interpretation: This verse, a stern declaration, speaks to the consequences of disbelief and wrongdoing. It clearly states that Allah will not pardon or guide those who reject His message and commit injustice.  The implication is that such actions, combined with a rejection of faith, sever the path to Allah's forgiveness and guidance.  It emphasizes the importance of faith and righteous conduct in securing God's mercy and blessings.  Crucially, it does not imply that Allah is unable to forgive, but rather that those who persist in these actions have placed themselves outside the scope of His forgiveness and guidance.  The verse serves as a warning and a reminder of the severe consequences of ignoring divine guidance and perpetuating unjust acts.
orig: إن الذين كفروا وظلموا لم يكن الله ليغفر لهم ولا ليهديهم طريقا

translation: Except for the way of Hell, wherein they will abide eternally. And that is easy for Allah.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the ultimate consequence of rejecting the path of righteousness and choosing to follow the path of sin and disobedience to Allah. It states that the only alternative to eternal bliss in Paradise is eternal punishment in Hellfire.  The phrase "except for the way of Hell" underscores the stark dichotomy between the two paths.  The eternal nature of Hell is highlighted by the words "abiding eternally."  The final part, "and that is easy for Allah," signifies that Allah has the absolute power and effortless ability to administer justice and enforce the consequences of one's choices. It emphasizes Allah's omnipotence and the inevitable reality of judgment. The verse serves as a warning and a reminder of the importance of choosing the right path, ultimately leading to eternal Paradise, and the inevitable consequences of a life of sin.  This is a verse that demonstrates God's justice, power, and mercy; justice in that He has laid out the path to paradise and the path to Hell, and power in that he is able to judge and enact these consequences.  It also displays mercy in that He offers the path to paradise, and warns us of the path to Hell, and thus gives us a chance to rectify our choices.  Ultimately, the choice is ours and the eternal destination is accordingly.
orig: إلا طريق جهنم خالدين فيها أبدا وكان ذلك على الله يسيرا

translation: O mankind, the Messenger has come to you with the truth from your Lord. So believe, for it is better for you. And if you disbelieve, then to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. And Allah is Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: This verse is a powerful call to faith in Islam. It addresses all humanity, emphasizing the arrival of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) as a messenger of God, bringing a message of truth and guidance. The verse asserts that accepting this message is inherently beneficial to humanity.  It is presented as a clear choice: embrace the truth and find betterment, or reject it and face the consequences. The final part highlights God's omnipotence and knowledge, reminding disbelievers that God possesses absolute control over everything and is fully aware of all actions. Ultimately, the verse emphasizes that the consequences of disbelief do not diminish God's power or wisdom, but rather underscore the inevitable outcome of rejecting divine guidance.
orig: يا أيها الناس قد جاءكم الرسول بالحق من ربكم فآمنوا خيرا لكم وإن تكفروا فإن لله ما في السماوات والأرض وكان الله عليما حكيما

translation: O People of the Book, do not exaggerate in your religion, and do not utter falsehood concerning Allah. The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, is but a messenger of Allah and His Word, which He bestowed upon Mary and a spirit from Him. Believe in Allah and His messengers and do not say "three." Cease; it is better for you. Indeed, Allah is One God; Glorified be He! It is not befitting for Him to have a son. His is whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And sufficient is Allah as a Disposer of affairs.
interpretation: This verse is a crucial clarification of the Christian concept of the Trinity, addressed directly to the People of the Book (Jews and Christians). It emphasizes the oneness of God (Tawhid) and the complete rejection of attributing any sort of divinity or sonship to God.  It challenges Christians to avoid over-emphasizing or distorting their beliefs regarding Jesus, emphasizing that Jesus was a human messenger of God, born of a virgin through divine intervention, and blessed by God's word and spirit, but ultimately a creation.  The verse criticizes the doctrine of the Trinity, arguing it is a form of polytheism, as it implies more than one divine entity.  It asserts that God is absolutely singular and unique, having no offspring or partners.  This verse is a fundamental Islamic tenet upholding the absolute oneness and transcendence of God (Allah).  The final phrase emphasizes Allah's complete sovereignty and the sufficiency of his guidance and power to resolve matters within creation.  The imperative to refrain from the concept of the Trinity is a call for adherence to the true monotheistic faith and avoids the pitfalls of associating partners with God. The verse also highlights the importance of recognizing prophets and messengers as part of God's plan to guide humanity.
orig: يا أهل الكتاب لا تغلوا في دينكم ولا تقولوا على الله إلا الحق إنما المسيح عيسى ابن مريم رسول الله وكلمته ألقاها إلى مريم وروح منه فآمنوا بالله ورسله ولا تقولوا ثلاثة انتهوا خيرا لكم إنما الله إله واحد سبحانه أن يكون له ولد له ما في السماوات وما في الأرض وكفى بالله وكيلا

translation: The Messiah will not be reluctant to be a servant of Allah, nor the honored angels.  And whoever is reluctant to worship Him and is arrogant, He will gather them all to Him.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute submission and servitude of Jesus (peace be upon him) and the angels to Allah.  It highlights their inherent willingness to serve God, contrasting this with the arrogance and refusal of those who reject worshiping Him.  The phrase "He will gather them all to Him" indicates a final judgment where everyone, including those who have shown reluctance and arrogance, will be accountable for their actions before God. This verse is important because it affirms the importance of faith and humility, and the inevitable reckoning for all on the Day of Judgment.
orig: لن يستنكف المسيح أن يكون عبدا لله ولا الملائكة المقربون ومن يستنكف عن عبادته ويستكبر فسيحشرهم إليه جميعا

translation: But those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will grant them their rewards in full, and increase for them from His bounty. But as for those who shunned and were arrogant, We will punish them with a painful punishment, and they will find no protector or helper besides Allah.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the differing fates awaiting believers and disbelievers.  It highlights the fundamental concept of reward and punishment in Islam.  Those who have faith (aiman) and perform righteous deeds (amal al-salihat) will receive full recompense from Allah, and even further blessings and bounty.  This signifies that Allah's rewards are not only just but also abundant for those who strive towards His pleasure.  In contrast, those who turn away from faith, choosing arrogance (istankaf and istikbar), will face a severe and painful punishment.  Importantly, this verse emphasizes that such individuals will find no refuge or support against Allah's judgment, highlighting the ultimate power and sovereignty of God.  This juxtaposition emphasizes the fundamental choice humanity faces and the consequences that flow from it; faith and righteous action lead to divine favour, while rejection and arrogance bring divine retribution.  The specific forms of this reward and punishment are not detailed, leaving room for divine wisdom in their manifestation.  The overall message is one of accountability and the importance of aligning oneself with God's will.
orig: فأما الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات فيوفيهم أجورهم ويزيدهم من فضله وأما الذين استنكفوا واستكبروا فيعذبهم عذابا أليما ولا يجدون لهم من دون الله وليا ولا نصيرا

translation: O mankind, there has come to you a clear proof from your Lord, and We have sent down to you a manifest light.
interpretation: This verse serves as a powerful call to humanity. It proclaims the arrival of undeniable evidence, a clear sign of divine guidance, from God. This sign is not abstract or hidden; rather, it is presented in a manifest and illuminating way, as a ‘نور مبين’ (manifest light).  This light, often interpreted as the Quran itself, is a comprehensive guide, providing clear laws, morals, and a path to understanding the divine. The verse is urging acceptance of this evidence and adhering to the guidance it provides, as it represents a crucial turning point in humanity's relationship with their Creator, offering a means to enlightenment and a better understanding of existence. It highlights the importance of seeking and responding to divine revelation, which is presented in a clear and easily understandable way for all to benefit from.
orig: يا أيها الناس قد جاءكم برهان من ربكم وأنزلنا إليكم نورا مبينا

translation: But as for those who believe in God and hold fast to Him, He will admit them to His mercy and bounty, and will guide them to a straight path.
interpretation: This verse highlights the profound connection between faith in God, adherence to His guidance, and the blessings that follow.  It emphasizes that those who truly believe in Allah and strive to live according to His teachings will experience His mercy and generosity.  This isn't merely a promise of earthly prosperity, but a broader concept encompassing spiritual fulfillment and a clear path towards a righteous life.  "Holding fast to Him" (اعتصموا به) implies active engagement and adherence to Islamic principles, not just a passive belief. The verse assures those who commit themselves to this path that God will grant them His grace, abundance, and ultimately, a straight path leading to His pleasure and eternal reward. The "straight path" (صراطا مستقيما) signifies the righteous way of life in Islam, which includes submission to God's will and seeking His guidance in all aspects of life.
orig: فأما الذين آمنوا بالله واعتصموا به فسيدخلهم في رحمة منه وفضل ويهديهم إليه صراطا مستقيما

translation: They ask you about inheritance in cases of a deceased with no children and a sister.  If a man dies leaving no child and a sister, then she inherits half of what he left.  He inherits her if she has no child.  If there are two sisters, then they inherit two-thirds of what he left.  If there are brothers and sisters, male and female, the male receives a share equivalent to the share of two females. God clarifies this for you so that you do not go astray.  God has knowledge of all things.
interpretation: This verse of the Quran addresses the intricate issue of inheritance when a person dies leaving no children.  It specifically outlines the shares of the deceased's relatives, ensuring a just distribution of wealth according to Islamic law.  The key points are that a deceased's sister inherits if there are no children. The share for a sister is half the estate if there is only one sister.  If there are two sisters, their combined share is two-thirds.  Crucially, the verse establishes the principle of differentiated inheritance based on gender, where a male's share is twice that of a female's. This is for situations involving brothers and sisters. This verse is not meant to condone inequality but to ensure equitable distribution in different scenarios. Importantly, the verse emphasizes that God clarifies these rules to prevent misunderstanding and error in the process.  The overall message is one of divine guidance and equitable distribution of wealth and inheritance, acknowledging gender distinctions in a manner that maintains fairness within the framework of Islamic law.
orig: يستفتونك قل الله يفتيكم في الكلالة إن امرؤ هلك ليس له ولد وله أخت فلها نصف ما ترك وهو يرثها إن لم يكن لها ولد فإن كانتا اثنتين فلهما الثلثان مما ترك وإن كانوا إخوة رجالا ونساء فللذكر مثل حظ الأنثيين يبين الله لكم أن تضلوا والله بكل شيء عليم

translation: O you who have believed, fulfill the contracts.  Lawful for you are the domesticated animals, except for what is recited to you, forbidden (game), and you are forbidden (from hunting them).  Allah decrees what He wills.
interpretation: This verse addresses Muslims, emphasizing the importance of upholding contracts and agreements.  It clarifies the permissibility of consuming domesticated livestock, differentiating it from hunted game. The specific types of forbidden game are those explicitly mentioned in the Quran.  The verse ultimately highlights Allah's absolute authority and His prerogative in determining laws and regulations.  The prohibition on hunting the mentioned game likely serves a purpose within the broader context of preserving wildlife resources, fostering sustainability, and establishing a system of permissible and prohibited activities.  It is important to note that the specifics of 'what is recited to you' likely refer to the Quranic verses detailing prohibited game, rather than a general concept of 'forbidden' in all cases. The concept of 'Allah decrees what He wills' reinforces that these rules are divinely ordained, not arbitrary human constructs.
orig: يا أيها الذين آمنوا أوفوا بالعقود أحلت لكم بهيمة الأنعام إلا ما يتلى عليكم غير محلي الصيد وأنتم حرم إن الله يحكم ما يريد

translation: O you who have believed, do not invalidate the rituals of Allah or the sacred month or the [sacrificial] offering or the garlands or those who seek refuge in the Sacred Mosque, seeking favor from their Lord and [His] pleasure. And when you have performed your pilgrimage, hunt. Let not hatred of a people who have prevented you from the Sacred Mosque lead you to transgression. And cooperate in righteousness and piety, but do not cooperate in sin and aggression. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in penalty.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the sanctity of Allah's rituals, specifically highlighting the importance of respecting the sacred months, the sacrificial animals, the garments used during pilgrimage, and those seeking refuge in the Masjid al-Haram (the Grand Mosque in Mecca). It instructs believers to uphold these sacred practices and not violate them.  It prohibits actions that could disrupt the peace and sanctity of the Hajj (pilgrimage) and the surrounding environment.  The verse strongly discourages retaliation against those who might impede one's access to the mosque, emphasizing the need for maintaining righteousness and piety, rather than succumbing to anger and aggression.  The overall message is one of upholding ethical conduct, respectful behavior, and the avoidance of transgression, even in the face of adversity.  It promotes unity and cooperation in virtuous acts, but cautions against participation in sinful or unjust activities. The ultimate message is to prioritize piety and fear Allah's judgment.  The verse is essentially outlining a code of conduct for pilgrims and those within the sacred space, encouraging peaceful interactions and reinforcing the importance of maintaining the sanctity of the sacred month and place.  It also emphasizes the importance of maintaining a respectful relationship with others, even when faced with opposition.
orig: يا أيها الذين آمنوا لا تحلوا شعائر الله ولا الشهر الحرام ولا الهدي ولا القلائد ولا آمين البيت الحرام يبتغون فضلا من ربهم ورضوانا وإذا حللتم فاصطادوا ولا يجرمنكم شنآن قوم أن صدوكم عن المسجد الحرام أن تعتدوا وتعاونوا على البر والتقوى ولا تعاونوا على الإثم والعدوان واتقوا الله إن الله شديد العقاب

translation: Forbidden to you are the dead animal, blood, the flesh of the pig, and what has been slaughtered for other than Allah, the strangled animal, the beaten animal, the fallen animal, the animal struck by a blunt instrument, and what the beasts of prey have devoured, except what you have slaughtered, and what has been sacrificed on raised altars.  Forbidden also is divination by arrows. That is transgression. Today, those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion. So do not fear them, and fear Me (Allah).  Today, I have perfected your religion for you and completed My favour upon you, and have chosen Islam as your religion.  But whoever is compelled by necessity, without deliberate wrongdoing, then Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation:
This verse from Surah Al-Ma'idah (The Table Spread) lays down prohibitions on certain foods and practices, essentially outlining dietary laws and clarifying Islamic principles regarding faith and community.  

The initial prohibitions on specific animals (dead, blood, pig, etc.) are rooted in hygienic considerations but also reflect the concept of purity and divine sovereignty in the Islamic worldview.  These restrictions are designed to promote ethical behavior and distinguish Muslims from other religious and cultural practices.  The explicit prohibition against sacrificing to entities other than Allah emphasizes the oneness of God (Tawhid). 

The prohibition against divination by arrows is a clear condemnation of practices associated with idolatry and seeking guidance from sources other than God.  This verse establishes the ultimate sovereignty of Allah in all matters. 

The statement, "Today I have perfected your religion," is a significant theological declaration. It signifies that Islam has attained its complete form and divine guidance, but also underscores a continuing process of understanding and adherence.  

The verse transitions to a declaration of unwavering faith.  Muslims are instructed to be steadfast and not afraid of the disbelievers who oppose the religion. Instead, they are encouraged to fear Allah (God) and seek His pleasure.  The concluding verses highlight the mercy and forgiveness of God.   A person in dire need (who is 'compelled by necessity'), without willingly committing sin, is granted a degree of leniency in adhering to the law. This demonstrates the compassion and understanding embedded within Islamic teachings. The concept of "necessity" in this context is critical; it is not a carte blanche for violating the dietary laws but rather a nuanced understanding of how to balance divine commands with the practicalities of life.
orig: حرمت عليكم الميتة والدم ولحم الخنزير وما أهل لغير الله به والمنخنقة والموقوذة والمتردية والنطيحة وما أكل السبع إلا ما ذكيتم وما ذبح على النصب وأن تستقسموا بالأزلام ذلكم فسق اليوم يئس الذين كفروا من دينكم فلا تخشوهم واخشون اليوم أكملت لكم دينكم وأتممت عليكم نعمتي ورضيت لكم الإسلام دينا فمن اضطر في مخمصة غير متجانف لإثم فإن الله غفور رحيم

translation: They ask you what is lawful for them. Say, "Lawful for you are the good things, and what you have trained of the hunting animals, which you teach them as Allah has taught you. So eat from what they catch for you, and mention the name of Allah over it, and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is swift in account.
interpretation: This verse addresses the permissibility of certain foods and actions related to hunting.  It clarifies that generally, good and wholesome foods are lawful.  Crucially, it introduces a specific condition regarding hunting:  only animals that have been trained by humans, and taught the specific hunting techniques by Allah, are considered permissible. This suggests that animals hunted through natural instincts or trapping methods, without knowledge and training bestowed by God's (through human intervention) instructions, are not included. The phrase "what you have trained of the hunting animals" implies a level of human responsibility and skill in hunting.  The verse also emphasizes the importance of invoking Allah's name (ذكر اسم الله عليه) over the hunted game before consuming it, a ritual act that acknowledges Allah's ownership of all creation and His role in the provision. The final part, "and fear Allah," reinforces the overall theme of piety and responsibility.   It connects lawful food consumption with a deep sense of spiritual awareness and reverence for God.  The concluding statement, "Indeed, Allah is swift in account," serves as a reminder that God is aware of every action and will judge accordingly. This highlights the importance of adhering to the guidelines outlined in the verse to ensure ethical and pious conduct throughout the entire process of acquiring and consuming the hunted game. Therefore, the verse emphasizes the importance of righteousness and spiritual awareness in all aspects of life, from the simplest actions to the most complex ones.
orig: يسألونك ماذا أحل لهم قل أحل لكم الطيبات وما علمتم من الجوارح مكلبين تعلمونهن مما علمكم الله فكلوا مما أمسكن عليكم واذكروا اسم الله عليه واتقوا الله إن الله سريع الحساب

translation: This day are lawful unto you the good things, and the food of the people of the Scripture is lawful unto you, and your food is lawful unto them. And (lawful unto you, in marriage) are the chaste believing women and the chaste women of those who received the Scripture before you, when you give them their dowries, being chaste, not committing lewdness nor taking them as secret lovers. And whoever disbelieves in the faith, then his work is vain, and he will be, in the Hereafter, among the losers.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah al-Ma'ida (The Table Spread), deals with the permissibility of certain foods and marriages.  It establishes that food from the People of the Book (Jews and Christians) is permissible for Muslims, and vice-versa.  Crucially, it emphasizes that this extends to marriage, allowing Muslims to marry chaste women from the People of the Book, provided the marriage contract is fulfilled, with the payment of the dowry.  The verse emphasizes the importance of chastity and proper conduct in marriage, explicitly forbidding lewdness and illicit relationships.  It ultimately emphasizes the importance of faith; rejecting faith results in wasted effort and ultimate loss in the afterlife.
orig: اليوم أحل لكم الطيبات وطعام الذين أوتوا الكتاب حل لكم وطعامكم حل لهم والمحصنات من المؤمنات والمحصنات من الذين أوتوا الكتاب من قبلكم إذا آتيتموهن أجورهن محصنين غير مسافحين ولا متخذي أخدان ومن يكفر بالإيمان فقد حبط عمله وهو في الآخرة من الخاسرين

translation: O you who have believed, when you intend to pray, wash your faces and hands up to your elbows, and wipe your heads and feet up to your ankles. And if you are in a state of major impurity (janabah), purify yourselves. And if you are ill or on a journey, or one of you comes from the toilet, or you have touched women, and you do not find water, then use clean, dry earth (tayammum) to wipe your faces and hands. Allah intends no hardship for you, but He intends to purify you and complete His favor upon you that you may be grateful.
interpretation: This verse from Surah Al-Maida (5:6) outlines the ablutions (wudu) and the alternative practice of tayammum (dry ablution) in Islam.  It emphasizes the importance of ritual purity before prayer, and it provides guidelines for those who might not have access to water.  The verse underscores that these rituals are not meant to be burdensome, but rather to cleanse and purify the body and soul, thereby fostering a spiritual connection with Allah.  It highlights the divine mercy in providing an alternative to the standard ablution when water is scarce due to illness, travel, or other circumstances. The emphasis on gratitude (shukr) at the end underscores the importance of acknowledging and appreciating Allah's blessings, including the ability to practice prayer in any circumstance.  The verse also details the specific areas of cleansing for both wudu and tayammum, showing the meticulous nature of Islamic rituals while acknowledging the practicalities and potential challenges associated with them.
orig: يا أيها الذين آمنوا إذا قمتم إلى الصلاة فاغسلوا وجوهكم وأيديكم إلى المرافق وامسحوا برءوسكم وأرجلكم إلى الكعبين وإن كنتم جنبا فاطهروا وإن كنتم مرضى أو على سفر أو جاء أحد منكم من الغائط أو لامستم النساء فلم تجدوا ماء فتيمموا صعيدا طيبا فامسحوا بوجوهكم وأيديكم منه ما يريد الله ليجعل عليكم من حرج ولكن يريد ليطهركم وليتم نعمته عليكم لعلكم تشكرون

translation: And remember Allah's favor upon you and His covenant with you, when you said, "We hear and we obey." And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts.
interpretation: This verse is a reminder to Muslims of a crucial moment in their faith history.  It refers to the pivotal declaration of acceptance and obedience (سمعنا وأطعنا – *sama`na wa aṭa`na*) made by the early Muslims. This declaration, essentially promising to listen and obey Allah's commands, represents a fundamental covenant (ميثاق – *mīṭhāq*).  The verse emphasizes that Allah is well aware of the sincerity and intentions behind such commitments.  It is a reminder that true faith involves not just outward actions, but also genuine inner acceptance and commitment.  The verse connects the blessings bestowed upon Muslims (نعمة الله – *ni`mat Allāh*) directly to their fulfillment of this covenant.  Furthermore, it emphasizes the importance of fear of Allah (اتقوا الله – *itqū Allāh*) as a guiding principle to maintain sincerity and avoid hypocrisy.  The phrase "what is within the breasts" (ذات الصدور – *dhāt al-ṣudūr*) highlights Allah's knowledge of the hidden motivations and intentions, thus encouraging honesty and integrity in one's faith, beyond mere outward declarations.  In essence, the verse underscores the importance of internalizing and acting upon the covenant of faith, and remaining mindful of Allah's profound awareness of one's heart and intentions.
orig: واذكروا نعمة الله عليكم وميثاقه الذي واثقكم به إذ قلتم سمعنا وأطعنا واتقوا الله إن الله عليم بذات الصدور

translation: O you who have believed, be upholders of justice for God, witnesses to fairness. Let not hatred of a people incite you to depart from justice. Be just; that is nearer to piety. And fear God; God is aware of what you do.
interpretation: This verse from the Quran addresses believers, encouraging them to uphold justice and fairness in all their dealings.  It stresses the importance of maintaining a steadfast commitment to justice, even when facing opposition or animosity from others.  Hatred or prejudice should never be a justification for abandoning righteousness.  The verse emphasizes that acting justly is inherently closer to piety and a devout relationship with God.  Ultimately, God is aware of all actions and will hold individuals accountable.  The verse thus highlights the importance of individual moral responsibility and the necessity of upholding fairness as a cornerstone of faith.
orig: يا أيها الذين آمنوا كونوا قوامين لله شهداء بالقسط ولا يجرمنكم شنآن قوم على ألا تعدلوا اعدلوا هو أقرب للتقوى واتقوا الله إن الله خبير بما تعملون

translation: Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: This verse highlights the fundamental principle of reward and punishment in Islam.  Allah promises forgiveness and a substantial reward (a great reward, "ajr 'azim") to those who demonstrate faith (iman) and act upon righteous deeds (amal al-salihat).  Faith, in this context, isn't just a declaration of belief, but a lived experience reflected in good actions.  The promise of forgiveness underscores God's mercy and compassion, while the promise of a great reward emphasizes the eternal value of virtuous conduct.  It's a powerful incentive to strive for righteousness, knowing that Allah will acknowledge and recompense those efforts.  This verse emphasizes the importance of both faith and action in earning Allah's favor and reward, and forms a core tenet of Islamic morality.
orig: وعد الله الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات لهم مغفرة وأجر عظيم

translation: And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, those are the companions of the Fire.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah al-Kahf (The Cave), addresses those who reject the divine revelations and messages presented in the Quran.  It clearly states that such disbelievers, who reject the signs (ayah) of Allah, are destined for the Hellfire (Jahannam).  The term 'signs' (ayah) encompasses not only miracles and phenomenal events but also the fundamental truths and guidance presented in the scripture itself, logical arguments, and the very nature of creation around them.  The verse serves as a warning, highlighting the consequences of rejecting divine truth and the importance of accepting and believing in Allah's message.  It underscores the concept of accountability in the afterlife and the fundamental truth of the Quran's revelation. It also implies that those who deny or dismiss Allah's signs are ultimately responsible for their fate, and Allah will hold them accountable for their choices and actions.
orig: والذين كفروا وكذبوا بآياتنا أولئك أصحاب الجحيم

translation: O you who have believed, remember Allah's favor upon you when a people intended to extend their hands to you, but He restrained their hands from you. And fear Allah. And upon Allah let the believers rely.
interpretation: This verse recounts a historical event where a group of people intended to harm the believers.  Allah, through His divine power, prevented them from carrying out their malicious intent.  The verse serves as a reminder of Allah's protection and constant support for believers.  It encourages them to express gratitude for His blessings, particularly in times of peril.  The instruction to "fear Allah" implies recognizing His power and seeking His protection through obedience and piety.  Finally, the verse emphasizes the importance of relying on Allah and not on human strength or worldly power.  The believers' trust and reliance should be solely in Allah, understanding that He is the ultimate protector and provider.
orig: يا أيها الذين آمنوا اذكروا نعمت الله عليكم إذ هم قوم أن يبسطوا إليكم أيديهم فكف أيديهم عنكم واتقوا الله وعلى الله فليتوكل المؤمنون

translation: Indeed, Allah took a covenant from the Children of Israel, and We appointed twelve leaders among them.  Allah said, 'Indeed, I am with you if you establish prayer, give zakah, believe in My messengers, and support them, and loan Allah a good loan. I will surely forgive your sins and admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow. But whoever disbelieves after that from among you has strayed from the right path.'
interpretation:
This verse highlights a crucial covenant (agreement) Allah made with the Israelites.  It emphasizes a conditional promise of reward for obedience and a warning of straying from the path for disobedience.  The covenant involves several key obligations: 

* **Establishing prayer (صلاة):**  This fundamental act of worship underscores a consistent connection with the divine. 

* **Giving Zakat (زكاة):** This obligatory charitable giving promotes social justice and alleviates poverty, reflecting a responsibility towards the community. 

* **Belief in Allah's messengers (رسل):** This signifies acceptance of divine revelation and guidance throughout history.  Following these prophets is a key aspect of faith. 

* **Supporting Allah's messengers:**  This implies active support for the prophets and their mission, perhaps through guidance, protection, or spreading the message. 

* **Loaning Allah a good loan (إقراض الله قرضا حسنا):** This unusual phrase likely refers to voluntary acts of charity, generosity, and selfless service to humanity, recognizing these acts as loans to God.  The 'good loan' emphasizes the intention and purity of the deed. 

The verse promises forgiveness of sins and entry into Paradise (gardens beneath rivers) for those who fulfill these obligations. Conversely, it warns that those who disbelieve or abandon these commitments will stray from the correct path, facing potential consequences.  The emphasis on the covenant and the conditions reflects the importance of maintaining a strong relationship with God and His messengers for a righteous life and a better hereafter.
orig: ولقد أخذ الله ميثاق بني إسرائيل وبعثنا منهم اثني عشر نقيبا وقال الله إني معكم لئن أقمتم الصلاة وآتيتم الزكاة وآمنتم برسلي وعزرتموهم وأقرضتم الله قرضا حسنا لأكفرن عنكم سيئاتكم ولأدخلنكم جنات تجري من تحتها الأنهار فمن كفر بعد ذلك منكم فقد ضل سواء السبيل

translation: So because they broke their covenant, We cursed them and hardened their hearts. They distort the words from their proper places, and they forgot a portion of that with which they were reminded.  And there will continually emerge treachery from them, except for a few among them. So pardon them and overlook [their faults], indeed Allah loves the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse describes the consequences of breaking a covenant or agreement with God.  The breaking of the covenant is described as causing God to curse them and to harden their hearts.  This hardening of the heart is a spiritual condition where one's understanding and awareness of God and His message become dulled or distorted.  The phrase "They distort the words from their proper places" refers to the manipulation of religious teachings, misinterpreting them, or deliberately deviating from the true meaning.  The act of forgetting a portion of the message implies negligence, disinterest, or a deliberate turning away from guidance.  Despite this pervasive treachery, there is a saving grace in that it does not manifest in all. This is followed by a divine imperative to forgive and overlook the shortcomings of those who have strayed, because Allah loves those who do good.  This passage highlights God's mercy and compassion, even in the face of human betrayal and transgression, and emphasizes the importance of forgiveness and tolerance in the face of persistent faults, as long as there is evidence of genuine repentance.
orig: فبما نقضهم ميثاقهم لعناهم وجعلنا قلوبهم قاسية يحرفون الكلم عن مواضعه ونسوا حظا مما ذكروا به ولا تزال تطلع على خائنة منهم إلا قليلا منهم فاعف عنهم واصفح إن الله يحب المحسنين

translation: And of those who said, 'We are Christians,' We took their covenant, but they forgot a portion of that which they were reminded of. So We stirred up enmity and hatred between them until the Day of Resurrection. And Allah will inform them of what they used to do.
interpretation: This verse addresses a specific group, those who claim to be Christians. It highlights a crucial aspect of their past actions: a covenant, or agreement, made with God.  Crucially, this covenant was not upheld in its entirety; they forgot, or neglected, parts of the teachings and obligations that were established in that agreement.  As a consequence of this breach of trust, a deliberate policy of discord and antagonism was set in place between them and others.  This division, marked by enmity and hatred, persists until the Day of Judgment.  The verse emphasizes the ultimate accountability of these individuals and their actions.  It suggests that their deeds, both remembered and forgotten, will be revealed and judged by God on the Day of Judgment.  The key takeaway is that neglecting or forgetting parts of one's agreement with God has consequences, and that God ultimately holds all accountable for their actions.
orig: ومن الذين قالوا إنا نصارى أخذنا ميثاقهم فنسوا حظا مما ذكروا به فأغرينا بينهم العداوة والبغضاء إلى يوم القيامة وسوف ينبئهم الله بما كانوا يصنعون

translation: O People of the Book, Our Messenger has come to you, clarifying for you much of what you used to conceal from the Book, and pardoning much. Indeed, light and a clear Book have come to you from Allah.
interpretation: This verse, addressed to the People of the Book (Jews and Christians), signifies the arrival of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) as a messenger of God.  It highlights a crucial role of his prophethood: to unveil the obscured or misinterpreted parts of their scriptures (the Torah and Gospel).  The phrase "clarifying for you much of what you used to conceal from the Book" suggests that some aspects of the divine message were either deliberately hidden or mistakenly overlooked by those communities.  This implies a degree of corruption or misinterpretation within their scripture and religious practice.  "And pardoning much" indicates that God's mercy and forgiveness are extended, overlooking past errors and differences. The verse further emphasizes the divine source of Islam, introducing it as a light and clear Book (the Quran), demonstrating the continuity and completion of the divine message previously revealed through the scriptures of the People of the Book. Ultimately, the verse serves as a call to embrace the complete and perfected revelation of God, as presented through the Quran, and for a renewed understanding of God's message and guidance.
orig: يا أهل الكتاب قد جاءكم رسولنا يبين لكم كثيرا مما كنتم تخفون من الكتاب ويعفو عن كثير قد جاءكم من الله نور وكتاب مبين

translation: By it [the Qur'an] Allah guides whom He wills of those who seek His pleasure along the paths of peace. He brings them out of darkness into light by His permission, and guides them to a straight path.
interpretation: This verse highlights the Qur'an's role as a guide to those who seek Allah's pleasure.  It emphasizes that guidance is a divine act, bestowed by Allah upon those who sincerely desire it.  The phrase "paths of peace" (سبل السلام) suggests a holistic path towards tranquility and well-being, encompassing spiritual, social, and moral aspects.  The transition from "darkness" (الظلمات) to "light" (النور) symbolizes the movement from ignorance, confusion, and spiritual blindness to knowledge, understanding, and enlightenment.  Crucially, Allah's permission and will are emphasized, meaning that the Qur'an's guidance is not automatic but rather a grace granted to those who actively seek it.  The phrase "straight path" (صراط مستقيم) refers to the path of righteousness and submission to Allah's will, a core concept in Islam.  In essence, the verse underscores the Qur'an's role as a means for achieving complete and lasting guidance toward a righteous life, but it is dependent on the individual's desire to embrace that guidance.
orig: يهدي به الله من اتبع رضوانه سبل السلام ويخرجهم من الظلمات إلى النور بإذنه ويهديهم إلى صراط مستقيم

translation: Indeed, those who said, "God is the Messiah, son of Mary," have disbelieved. Say, "Who can withhold anything from God if He intends to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary, and his mother, and everyone on earth?" To God belongs dominion over the heavens and the earth and everything between them. He creates what He wills. And God is capable of all things.
interpretation: This verse from Surah Al-Ma'ida (The Table Spread) addresses the disbelief of those who ascribe divinity to Jesus (peace be upon him), claiming that he is God himself.  It emphatically refutes this notion by highlighting God's absolute power and sovereignty.  The verse asserts that God, in His divine will and absolute power, holds control over all creation, including the life and death of anyone, even the Messiah, son of Mary.  The reference to the mother emphasizes that God's power extends to all individuals, regardless of status.  The verse reinforces the principle of tawhid (monotheism), emphasizing God's absolute control and power over all things. It underscores that God is the sole creator and ultimate authority, and any assertion of divinity for anyone else is a grave misbelief.  The verse effectively counters the misconception of Jesus' (peace be upon him) divine status by highlighting God's absolute power and control. This is a crucial aspect of Islamic theology, which upholds the oneness of God and Jesus' (peace be upon him) status as a prophet, not divine. Therefore, the verse serves as a clear refutation of those who associate divinity with anyone other than God.
orig: لقد كفر الذين قالوا إن الله هو المسيح ابن مريم قل فمن يملك من الله شيئا إن أراد أن يهلك المسيح ابن مريم وأمه ومن في الأرض جميعا ولله ملك السماوات والأرض وما بينهما يخلق ما يشاء والله على كل شيء قدير

translation: And the Jews and Christians say, "We are the children of God and His beloved." Say, "Then why has He not punished you for your sins?  Rather, you are humans, among those whom He created. He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. And to God belongs the dominion of the heavens, the earth, and that which is between them, and to Him is the eventual return."
interpretation: This verse is a powerful refutation of the Jewish and Christian claims of being God's children and His beloved in a unique, special way, implying divinity or a privileged status.  The verse points out the inherent absurdity of such claims.  It emphasizes that humans, including Jews and Christians, are created beings, subject to the same laws and accountable for their actions as all others.  God's power and judgment extend beyond the specific claims of any particular religious group.  He has the absolute power to forgive or punish as He sees fit.  This concept emphasizes the oneness of God (Tawhid) and His absolute sovereignty.  The verse highlights the importance of recognizing the inherent equality of all human beings, regardless of their religious beliefs, in the eyes of God.  The phrase "and to Him is the eventual return" serves as a reminder of the ultimate accountability that awaits all before God and underscores that God is the ultimate arbiter and judge in all affairs.
orig: وقالت اليهود والنصارى نحن أبناء الله وأحباؤه قل فلم يعذبكم بذنوبكم بل أنتم بشر ممن خلق يغفر لمن يشاء ويعذب من يشاء ولله ملك السماوات والأرض وما بينهما وإليه المصير

translation: O People of the Book, Our Messenger has come to you, clarifying for you, after a period of messengers, that you may say: "No good tidings or warner has come to us." Indeed, a bringer of good news and a warner has come to you. And Allah is over all things powerful.
interpretation: This verse is a direct address to the People of the Book (Jews and Christians).  It establishes the prophethood of the final messenger, Muhammad, as the culmination of a line of prophets.  The verse highlights the importance of accepting the message of Islam, arguing that a prophet has, in fact, arrived.  The phrase "after a period of messengers" (على فترة من الرسل) emphasizes that this is the final prophet in a sequence of messengers sent by God. It is a strong refutation of any claim that a new prophet was not needed, or that Muhammad's message was not authentic or timely.  The verse also points to the responsibility of those who receive the message. They cannot claim ignorance or dismissal of the messenger. They are called upon to accept the message of the new prophet, the bringer of good tidings (bashir), and warning (nazir), and acknowledge the power and sovereignty of God in all aspects of existence.  The verse is a call to faith and a clear statement of the completion of prophethood in Islam.  The finality of Muhammad's prophethood is being emphasized, setting him apart from the previous prophets, yet also emphasizing the continuity and universality of God's message throughout history.
orig: يا أهل الكتاب قد جاءكم رسولنا يبين لكم على فترة من الرسل أن تقولوا ما جاءنا من بشير ولا نذير فقد جاءكم بشير ونذير والله على كل شيء قدير

translation: And [remember] when Musa said to his people, "O my people, remember the favor of Allah upon you when He made among you prophets and made you kings, and gave you what He had not given any of the worlds (people)."
interpretation: This verse from Surah al-Baqarah (The Cow) exhorts the Israelites to reflect upon the profound blessings bestowed upon them by Allah.  Moses, upon him be peace, reminds them of the pivotal role prophets played in their lives, guiding them towards the divine path.  The mention of 'kings' likely refers to the leadership structure established during that time.  Crucially, the verse highlights the unique and unparalleled favors Allah granted the Israelites: the gift of prophethood, kingship, and worldly blessings that no other nation had been similarly favored with.  The phrase "what He had not given any of the worlds" emphasizes the exceptional generosity of Allah towards this particular people.  It serves as a reminder of Allah's favor and mercy, but also of their responsibility to appreciate and act upon those blessings.  This verse is a call to gratitude and remembrance, and implies a warning to avoid ingratitude, which would lead to the loss of these blessings and divine favor.
orig: وإذ قال موسى لقومه يا قوم اذكروا نعمة الله عليكم إذ جعل فيكم أنبياء وجعلكم ملوكا وآتاكم ما لم يؤت أحدا من العالمين

translation: O my people, enter the holy land which Allah has decreed for you, and do not turn back on your heels, lest you become losers.
interpretation: This verse, likely addressed to the Israelites, urges them to enter the promised land, the land of Palestine, as divinely ordained.  It emphasizes the importance of unwavering commitment and forward movement.  Turning back, a metaphor for abandoning the divine purpose or losing courage, is condemned as a path to loss and failure. The verse carries a strong message of faith, obedience, and the importance of fulfilling divine directives.  It likely refers to a specific historical context in which the Israelites were either hesitating or turning away from their divinely ordained journey. The concept of 'holy land' is central to many Abrahamic faiths and holds a deep spiritual significance, highlighting God's chosenness and promise to his people.
orig: يا قوم ادخلوا الأرض المقدسة التي كتب الله لكم ولا ترتدوا على أدباركم فتنقلبوا خاسرين

translation: They said, "O Moses, there are arrogant people within it, and we will not enter it until they leave it. If they leave it, then we will enter it."
interpretation: This verse describes a situation where a group of people are hesitant to enter a specific place (likely a city or a land) because of the presence of powerful, oppressive, or arrogant inhabitants. They explicitly state their condition for entering: the removal of these dominant figures.  It signifies a struggle for power or control, and a refusal to submit to injustice or oppression.  The verse underscores the importance of freedom from tyranny and the desire for a just environment. The context likely involves a dispute or a conflict over resources or territory. Moses' people likely face an existential threat from the powerful people and are seeking security and a path to peacefully coexist and settle in the land, which will only be possible after the removal of the dominating power(s).
orig: قالوا يا موسى إن فيها قوما جبارين وإنا لن ندخلها حتى يخرجوا منها فإن يخرجوا منها فإنا داخلون

translation: Two men, from among those who fear the bounty of Allah upon them, said, "Enter the gate from there. When you enter it, you will be victorious. And upon Allah, rely, if you are believers."
interpretation: This verse, likely from a narrative in the Quran, depicts a moment of strategic planning and exhortation. Two individuals, conscious of God's favor and possessing piety, are providing guidance.  They instruct others to enter a specific location (the gate). This suggests a military or similar critical situation where entering a strategic point is crucial for victory. The phrase, "When you enter it, you will be victorious," highlights the importance of tactical execution and the trust in Allah's blessings. The final part, "And upon Allah, rely, if you are believers," underscores the fundamental importance of faith and trust in God's plan. It signifies that victory is ultimately a gift from Allah, and it is contingent upon the believers' faith and submission to His will. The passage suggests a potential battle or a confrontation, where strategic entry and reliance on divine support are paramount for success.  The context of the surrounding verses would greatly enhance a more precise understanding.
orig: قال رجلان من الذين يخافون أنعم الله عليهما ادخلوا عليهم الباب فإذا دخلتموه فإنكم غالبون وعلى الله فتوكلوا إن كنتم مؤمنين

translation: They said, "O Moses, we will never enter it as long as they are in it. So go you and your Lord and fight, while we remain here seated."
interpretation: This verse describes the Israelites' response to Moses' call to enter the Promised Land (likely referring to Canaan).  They express fear and unwillingness to engage in the impending conflict against the inhabitants.  They acknowledge the necessity of fighting, but place the responsibility and the burden of action squarely on Moses and God. They essentially refuse to participate, choosing passivity and remaining behind.  Their statement highlights their lack of faith and courage in the face of the challenge ahead.  The verse contrasts their cowardice and faithlessness with Moses' and God's willingness to confront the situation.  It is a poignant example of how doubt and fear can paralyze even those claiming faith and how the actions and beliefs of individuals can affect the collective destiny of a community.
orig: قالوا يا موسى إنا لن ندخلها أبدا ما داموا فيها فاذهب أنت وربك فقاتلا إنا هاهنا قاعدون

translation: My Lord, I have power only over myself and my brother.  So separate us from the corrupting people.
interpretation: This verse, often attributed to Prophet Moses (Musa) in the context of his struggle with the Pharaoh and the corrupt society of Egypt, expresses a powerful sentiment of personal responsibility and limitation.  Moses acknowledges his inability to directly change the hearts or actions of the entire corrupt community. He recognizes that his influence is confined to his own person and that of his brother, Aaron (Harun).  He thus beseeches God to intervene and protect them from the corrupting influence of the Pharaoh's oppressive regime.  The verse highlights the importance of focusing on one's own righteous conduct and seeking divine intervention to mitigate the negative impact of others' wrongdoing.  It implicitly recognizes the limitations of individual agency in confronting large-scale societal corruption.  Ultimately, it emphasizes reliance on God's power to separate the righteous from the unjust.
orig: قال رب إني لا أملك إلا نفسي وأخي فافرق بيننا وبين القوم الفاسقين

translation: He said, "Indeed, it is forbidden to them for forty years, wandering about in the land. So do not grieve over the corrupting people."
interpretation: This verse, likely from the story of the Israelites, describes a divine decree forbidding a specific group, likely the Israelites, from entering a particular place or engaging in a specific activity for forty years.  The phrase "wandering about in the land" suggests a period of exile and punishment.  The command to "do not grieve over the corrupting people" implies a divine judgment upon their actions and a rejection of their ways.  The interpretation of the specific "it" (إنها) and the "corrupting people" (القوم الفاسقين) requires understanding the broader context of the narrative.  The verse emphasizes divine justice and the consequences of disobedience.  It also teaches a perspective of patience and detachment from the fate of those who have strayed from the righteous path.  The forty-year duration is a symbolic period, possibly representing a time of spiritual purification or societal reformation.  A key element is the divine perspective of the situation.  The narrative's central lesson might be about the need for adherence to divine commands, the consequences of transgression, and the eventual triumph of righteousness over corruption.
orig: قال فإنها محرمة عليهم أربعين سنة يتيهون في الأرض فلا تأس على القوم الفاسقين

translation: And recite to them the story of the sons of Adam in truth, when they offered a sacrifice. Acceptance was granted from one of them, but not from the other. The one said, "I will surely kill you." The other said, "Indeed, Allah only accepts from the righteous.
interpretation: This verse recounts a story from the early Islamic tradition, likely metaphorical, about the sons of Adam (Adam and Eve's children). It centers on the concept of acceptance by God and the importance of piety (taqwa).  The sacrifice, likely a symbolic act, represents a spiritual offering.  The story highlights a key theme in the Quran: God's judgment is based on inner piety and righteousness, not merely outward actions.  While the exact nature of the sacrifice and the specific sin of the rejected son are not detailed in the verse, it implies that the differing acceptance reflects an internal difference in faith and devotion.  The rejected son, motivated by envy or anger, is portrayed as acting out of worldly desires, rather than from a place of spiritual acceptance or faith.  Ultimately, the verse emphasizes that true acceptance comes from God, and He only accepts the offerings of those who are righteous and pious, focusing on the inner spiritual state and not just outward acts.  It's likely a parable intended to teach a lesson about the importance of righteous conduct, sincere devotion, and how God judges individuals based on their hearts rather than just their actions.
orig: واتل عليهم نبأ ابني آدم بالحق إذ قربا قربانا فتقبل من أحدهما ولم يتقبل من الآخر قال لأقتلنك قال إنما يتقبل الله من المتقين

translation: If you stretch out your hand to kill me, I will not stretch out my hand to you to kill you. Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: This verse, from the Quran (likely Surah al-Kahf, but without the full context, exact location is uncertain), describes a pivotal moment of restraint and peaceful resolve in a potentially violent encounter.  The speaker, likely Joseph or another prophet in a similar situation, refuses to reciprocate aggression.  Instead of retaliating, they prioritize fearing Allah and maintaining justice. The phrase 'Lord of the worlds' emphasizes the inherent importance of avoiding violence and respecting the divine order.  The core message is one of avoiding the cycle of retribution and prioritizing peace, even in the face of potential danger.  It's a powerful statement about faith, self-control, and trust in God's judgment.  The refusal to match violence with violence is a hallmark of prophetic conduct in the Quran, highlighting the higher moral ground of peaceful resistance and reliance on divine justice.
orig: لئن بسطت إلي يدك لتقتلني ما أنا بباسط يدي إليك لأقتلك إني أخاف الله رب العالمين

translation: Indeed, I intend that you bear my sin and your sin, so that you will be among the companions of the Fire. That is the reward for the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse, often cited in the context of the story of Prophet Moses and the people he was leading, highlights the concept of individual accountability and responsibility for one's actions.  It emphasizes that God does not hold individuals accountable for the sins of others.  The verse suggests a specific instance where the speaker (likely God, or a prophet acting on God's behalf) is expressing a potential consequence – the individual bearing the punishment for their own wrongdoing, as well as the possible sin of others who have gone astray, if they fail to repent. The statement "That is the reward for the wrongdoers" underscores the inevitable and just judgment that awaits those who persist in injustice. The emphasis on individual burden, rather than collective responsibility, reinforces the idea that each person is accountable for their own choices and actions and should strive to follow the righteous path.  The context surrounding this verse is crucial for a full understanding, but in general, it highlights the profound consequences of sin and the importance of personal righteousness. This concept of individual accountability is a recurring theme in the Quran, emphasizing the individual's role in their salvation and the gravity of their actions.
orig: إني أريد أن تبوء بإثمي وإثمك فتكون من أصحاب النار وذلك جزاء الظالمين

translation: He made his soul subservient to it, and killed his brother. So he became of the losers.
interpretation: This verse refers to the story of Cain and Abel. It highlights the devastating consequences of yielding to base desires and committing a heinous act like fratricide.  The phrase "He made his soul subservient to it" implies a conscious choice, a surrender to anger, jealousy, or other negative emotions that led to the murder. The verse emphasizes the eternal loss incurred by such actions, positioning Cain as a quintessential example of someone who lost their way, their inner peace, and ultimately, their future. It serves as a warning against the destructive nature of unchecked anger and the profound regret that often follows impulsive and violent acts.  The Qur'an, in this context, emphasizes the moral and spiritual repercussions of such choices. It contrasts this action against the potential for harmony and peace that should govern human relationships and interactions.
orig: فطوعت له نفسه قتل أخيه فقتله فأصبح من الخاسرين

translation: So Allah sent a raven, searching the earth to show him how to cover up the disgrace of his brother. He said, "Woe to me! Was I unable to be like this raven and cover up my brother's disgrace?" So he became one of the repentant.
interpretation: This verse, from the story of Cain and Abel, illustrates the consequences of murder and the emotional turmoil that follows.  Cain, after killing his brother Abel, is plagued by remorse and the profound sense of loss and the moral burden of his actions.  The raven, sent by God, acts as a symbolic representation of nature's response to crime.  It visually demonstrates the process of concealing death, showing Cain a tangible example of how to deal with the aftermath of his horrific act.  However, this demonstration is not a justification or a simple solution. Rather, it highlights the futility of trying to erase the consequences of his transgression.  Cain's self-recrimination and subsequent repentance underscore the deep emotional and moral impact of his crime. He recognizes his failure to act justly and to prevent the death of his brother.  He is not absolved of his actions, but the verse reveals God's compassion and the possibility of remorse, even for the most grievous sins. The verse emphasizes the gravity of murder and the lasting impact it has on the perpetrator, highlighting the importance of accountability and the path to repentance in the face of wrongdoing.  The raven serves as an example, showing the natural responses to loss, not as a way to justify Cain's actions, but as a reminder of the responsibility that comes with taking a life.
orig: فبعث الله غرابا يبحث في الأرض ليريه كيف يواري سوءة أخيه قال يا ويلتا أعجزت أن أكون مثل هذا الغراب فأواري سوءة أخي فأصبح من النادمين

translation: For that reason, We prescribed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul without [justification] for a soul, or [commits] corruption on the earth, it is as if he had killed all mankind. And whoever revives it, it is as if he had revived all mankind. Indeed, Our messengers came to them with clear evidence, but afterward, many of them were extravagant on the earth.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the profound value of human life and the gravity of taking it unjustly.  It establishes a strong moral imperative, equating the taking of an innocent life with the killing of all humanity.  The concept of "corruption on the earth" likely encompasses acts of injustice, oppression, and widespread harm.  The verse underscores that the Quranic law concerning this is not arbitrary but rather firmly rooted in justice and mercy. It further highlights that even with clear guidance from God's messengers, many individuals chose to act in ways that harmed themselves and others, effectively violating the fundamental principles presented.  This could be interpreted as a warning to subsequent generations, emphasizing the importance of maintaining justice and righteousness within society.  The verse links the preservation of life to the promotion of societal good, suggesting a direct correlation between individual actions and the overall well-being of the community. It's important to understand that "killing a soul" and "corruption" are broad terms encompassing a wide spectrum of actions and their impact, all of which are condemned by this verse.
orig: من أجل ذلك كتبنا على بني إسرائيل أنه من قتل نفسا بغير نفس أو فساد في الأرض فكأنما قتل الناس جميعا ومن أحياها فكأنما أحيا الناس جميعا ولقد جاءتهم رسلنا بالبينات ثم إن كثيرا منهم بعد ذلك في الأرض لمسرفون

translation: Indeed, the recompense of those who fight Allah and His Messenger and strive [with deceit] to make mischief throughout the land is that they are killed or crucified or have their hands and feet cut off from opposite sides or are exiled from the land. That is disgrace for them in this world, and for them in the hereafter is a great punishment.
interpretation: This verse outlines the consequences for those who actively oppose Allah and His Messenger (Muhammad) and engage in widespread corruption on Earth.  It's a strong statement about the seriousness of such actions.  The punishments mentioned – execution, crucifixion, amputation, and exile – are not arbitrary. They serve as a deterrent against societal disruption and a reminder of the divine justice that awaits those who undermine the established order. Importantly, these punishments are not meant to be seen as a call for personal vengeance, but rather as a divine response to severe transgressions against societal harmony.  They aim to protect the innocent, maintain order, and ultimately, deter others from similar behavior. The verse highlights the concept of accountability in the face of widespread harm.  The verse also stresses the eternal consequences of such actions, emphasizing that the disgrace and punishment in this world are only a prelude to a far more severe punishment in the hereafter. The specific type of punishment mentioned is based on the severity of the crime.  It suggests that a lesser crime might result in exile, while greater acts of rebellion and corruption might merit harsher penalties like execution or crucifixion.  The verse's emphasis on the impact on both this life and the next underscores the importance of righteous conduct in the eyes of Allah. Critically, the phrase 'striving to make mischief' ('yas'oona fi'l-ardhi fasada') emphasizes the intent and the scope of the transgression – it's not merely individual acts, but organized efforts to disrupt the social order.
orig: إنما جزاء الذين يحاربون الله ورسوله ويسعون في الأرض فسادا أن يقتلوا أو يصلبوا أو تقطع أيديهم وأرجلهم من خلاف أو ينفوا من الأرض ذلك لهم خزي في الدنيا ولهم في الآخرة عذاب عظيم

translation: Except for those who repented before you had power over them. Know that Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.
interpretation: This verse, found in the Quran, speaks to forgiveness and mercy within the context of warfare or conflict. It essentially states that those who had the opportunity to repent before being conquered or confronted will be forgiven by God. This implies a prior opportunity for those who committed wrong to seek forgiveness. The verse emphasizes that God's forgiveness and mercy are vast and extend to those who seek it, even if they acted against divine law or in a manner that might have warranted punishment.  Crucially, it suggests that the action of repentance itself can supersede the consequence of an action, especially if it occurs before any judgment or retaliation is enforced.  The phrase "before you had power over them" highlights the importance of repentance preceding any imposition of punishment or consequences.  It can also be seen as a counsel to those in power to be merciful and allow opportunities for repentance before resorting to harsher measures.  The verse, then, emphasizes God's boundless mercy and the possibility of redemption for those who seek it.
orig: إلا الذين تابوا من قبل أن تقدروا عليهم فاعلموا أن الله غفور رحيم

translation: O you who have believed, fear Allah and seek His means of approach. And strive in His cause that you may be successful.
interpretation:
This verse from Surah al-Mujadalah (The Argument) urges believers to adopt a comprehensive approach to achieving success in this life and the hereafter.  It outlines three crucial steps: 

1. **Fear Allah (itqaw Allah):** This isn't simply about avoiding sins, but encompasses a profound and reverent relationship with God.  It implies understanding His majesty, His knowledge, and His power.  This fear is not one of terror, but of respect and love, leading to a desire to please Him and act in accordance with His commands. 

2. **Seek His means of approach (tabtghu ilahi al-waseela):** This emphasizes the importance of striving to connect with God through various avenues.  This could include acts of worship like prayer (salat), supplication (dua), good deeds, charity (sadaqah), and seeking knowledge (ilm).  It highlights the active role of the believer in establishing a connection with Allah. This also implies avoiding obstacles or practices that hinder connection with God.

3. **Strive in His cause (jaahidu fi sabilihi):** This emphasizes the importance of active service to God's cause and upholding His values.  This includes the effort to spread justice, good morals, and to oppose injustice.  'Jihad' in this context isn't necessarily about physical conflict, but also about striving in the spiritual, intellectual, and social realms to uphold what is right and oppose what is wrong.  The verse connects striving with the potential for success (taflayhoon).  Success in this context encompasses spiritual, worldly, and ultimate success in the hereafter, all in accordance with Allah's will.  The ultimate reward for striving is success (falah), a state of happiness and fulfillment in this world and the next.

The verse, therefore, paints a picture of a holistic approach to faith. It underscores the need for piety, a deep connection with Allah, and active involvement in spreading goodness and opposing evil, all culminating in the ultimate goal of success and pleasing Allah.
orig: يا أيها الذين آمنوا اتقوا الله وابتغوا إليه الوسيلة وجاهدوا في سبيله لعلكم تفلحون

translation: Indeed, those who disbelieved, if they possessed all that is in the earth and the like of it with it, to ransom themselves from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted from them, and for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse highlights the futility of disbelief and the inability of wealth or material possessions to atone for rejecting faith on the Day of Judgment.  It emphasizes that earthly riches, no matter how abundant, cannot buy one's way out of divine retribution.  The punishment awaiting those who disbelieve is described as "painful," emphasizing its severity and the lasting consequences of their choices.  The verse underscores the importance of faith and righteous actions in the eyes of God, rather than material gain.  It serves as a warning and a reminder that true salvation lies in submission to God and adhering to His guidance, not in worldly accumulation.
orig: إن الذين كفروا لو أن لهم ما في الأرض جميعا ومثله معه ليفتدوا به من عذاب يوم القيامة ما تقبل منهم ولهم عذاب أليم

translation: They desire to emerge from the Fire, but they will not be able to emerge from it. And for them is a lasting punishment.
interpretation: This verse describes the desperate yet futile attempts of the disbelievers to escape the punishment of the Fire (Hell).  It highlights the irrevocable nature of God's judgment.  Their desire to escape is futile because they have committed actions that have earned them a permanent punishment.  The phrase "a lasting punishment" emphasizes the enduring and inescapable nature of the consequence.  The verse underscores the gravity of rejecting faith and the ultimate reality of the Divine judgment, emphasizing the importance of righteous action in this life as a means of avoiding eternal suffering.
orig: يريدون أن يخرجوا من النار وما هم بخارجين منها ولهم عذاب مقيم

translation: And the thief, male or female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they have earned, as a deterrent from Allah. And Allah is Exalted in Power, Wise.
interpretation: This verse from Surah Al-Ma'idah (The Table Spread) outlines a specific punishment for theft.  It's crucial to understand the context of the time and society when this verse was revealed.  The penalty of amputation was a prescribed punishment meant to deter further theft.  It was intended to protect the rights of individuals and the community's property by establishing a clear consequence.  While the literal application of amputation is no longer common due to changes in societal norms and legal systems, the core principle of accountability and the need for deterrents remain relevant. The verse emphasizes that this punishment, severe though it might appear, is divinely ordained to uphold justice and maintain societal order.  It underscores Allah's power (Azīz) and wisdom (Hakīm) in establishing such a system for justice and maintaining social equity.  Importantly, the punishment was specific to the act and did not apply to other crimes. The verse emphasizes the importance of upholding justice and maintaining a fair society.  The concept of 'nakala' (deterrent) is critical. The penalty served as a warning and discouragement to others contemplating similar actions.  Ultimately, the verse represents a specific legal framework from a specific time, highlighting God's wisdom in enacting justice and upholding a fair society.
orig: والسارق والسارقة فاقطعوا أيديهما جزاء بما كسبا نكالا من الله والله عزيز حكيم

translation: So whoever repents after his wrongdoing and amends, then Allah accepts his repentance. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the transformative power of repentance within Islam.  It emphasizes that even after committing wrong actions ('ظلم'), if a person sincerely repents ('تاب') and makes amends ('أصلح'), Allah will accept their repentance.  The verse highlights Allah's infinite mercy and forgiveness ('غفور رحيم').  It's not simply a passive forgiveness, but an active process of acceptance and restoration to a righteous path.  Crucially, the repentance must be accompanied by rectification of past wrongs.  It implies a sincere effort to undo the harm caused and to return to a righteous life.  This reinforces the importance of seeking forgiveness, striving for betterment, and the inherent mercy of God in Islam.
orig: فمن تاب من بعد ظلمه وأصلح فإن الله يتوب عليه إن الله غفور رحيم

translation: Haven't you known that Allah possesses dominion over the heavens and the earth? He afflicts whom He wills and forgives whom He wills. And Allah is over all things powerful.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute sovereignty and omnipotence of Allah. It asserts that Allah has complete control over the universe, including the heavens and the earth.  He is not bound by any limitations.  The phrase "afflicts whom He wills" does not imply a capricious or unjust system. Rather, it highlights that Allah's actions are based on His perfect wisdom and justice.  The forgiveness mentioned demonstrates His mercy and grace. He chooses whom to punish and whom to pardon, based on His knowledge that extends far beyond human comprehension. The final part, "and Allah is over all things powerful," reinforces the full extent of His ability to act as He sees fit within His perfect plan.  This verse is a reminder of Allah's complete control and emphasizes that all things ultimately rest in His hands. It serves to instill humility and reliance on Allah within the believer.
orig: ألم تعلم أن الله له ملك السماوات والأرض يعذب من يشاء ويغفر لمن يشاء والله على كل شيء قدير

translation: O Messenger, let not those who hasten in disbelief grieve you, those who say, "We believe" with their mouths, while their hearts do not believe, and those who follow Judaism, listening to falsehood, listening to other people who did not come to you, distorting words from their proper places, saying, 'If you are given this, take it, and if you are not given it, beware.'  And whoever Allah wills to cause to err, you will have no power over him from Allah. Those are the ones whom Allah does not will to purify their hearts. For them is disgrace in this world, and for them is a great punishment in the Hereafter.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) concerning the hypocrites and those who deliberately misinterpret or distort the divine message.  It assures him that he should not be disheartened by those who outwardly profess faith but inwardly reject it.  The verse specifically calls out the Jewish community who were listening to rumors and gossip, distorting the words of Allah from their proper context.  The core message is that true faith resides in the heart and that Allah is in ultimate control of who He guides and misguides. The verse emphasizes the consequences for those who deliberately distort and twist the divine message, both in this world and the next.  It is a reminder to the Prophet that his responsibility is to convey the message of Allah, and that success in guiding people is entirely up to Allah's will. Ultimately, Allah will judge the hearts, and those who intentionally reject or twist His message will face consequences in the hereafter.
orig: يا أيها الرسول لا يحزنك الذين يسارعون في الكفر من الذين قالوا آمنا بأفواههم ولم تؤمن قلوبهم ومن الذين هادوا سماعون للكذب سماعون لقوم آخرين لم يأتوك يحرفون الكلم من بعد مواضعه يقولون إن أوتيتم هذا فخذوه وإن لم تؤتوه فاحذروا ومن يرد الله فتنته فلن تملك له من الله شيئا أولئك الذين لم يرد الله أن يطهر قلوبهم لهم في الدنيا خزي ولهم في الآخرة عذاب عظيم

translation: Obeyers of falsehood, devourers of illicit gain! If they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them. If you turn away from them, they will not harm you at all. And if you judge, judge between them with justice. Indeed, Allah loves those who are just.
interpretation: This verse addresses a situation where a dispute arises before a Muslim leader, likely a judge or a person in a position of authority.  It criticizes those who seek falsehood and are involved in unlawful transactions (haram).  The verse emphasizes the importance of neutrality and detachment from the outcome of the judgement.  It instructs the leader not to be swayed by biased motivations or personal interests. If one can't make a fair decision, avoiding the dispute is acceptable, as their inaction won't result in any harm to them. Conversely, if they do decide to judge, the directive is to do so fairly and impartially, upholding justice.  This highlights the importance of justice and impartiality in Islamic law and governance.  The verse is a reminder that Allah favors those who are righteous and just in their dealings, a core principle in Islam.
orig: سماعون للكذب أكالون للسحت فإن جاءوك فاحكم بينهم أو أعرض عنهم وإن تعرض عنهم فلن يضروك شيئا وإن حكمت فاحكم بينهم بالقسط إن الله يحب المقسطين

translation: And how do they judge you, while with them is the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah? Then they turn away after that. And those are not the believers.
interpretation: This verse criticizes those who possess the Torah (the Jewish scripture), which contains divine judgments from Allah.  It accuses them of hypocrisy and inconsistency by possessing this knowledge of Allah's law yet rejecting or ignoring it when it conflicts with their desires or actions.  The phrase "they turn away after that" implies a deliberate and willful abandonment of the teachings of the Torah.  The verse ultimately concludes that such individuals, despite their possession of religious scripture, are not truly believers because their actions contradict their professed faith.  It highlights the importance of aligning one's actions with the divine guidance found in scripture, and that mere possession of religious knowledge is not enough to qualify someone as a believer.
orig: وكيف يحكمونك وعندهم التوراة فيها حكم الله ثم يتولون من بعد ذلك وما أولئك بالمؤمنين

translation: Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in it is guidance and light. By it, the prophets who submitted to Allah judge those who followed Judaism, the religious scholars, and the learned, concerning what they were entrusted of Allah's Book. And they were witnesses to it. So fear not mankind, but fear Me. And do not sell My verses for a low price. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, then they are the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the role of the Torah as a source of guidance and light, a divine book containing laws and principles for righteous living.  It highlights the prophets, rabbis, and scholars of Judaism as entrusted with upholding and interpreting this sacred text.  They were expected to judge disputes and matters of faith according to the Torah's teachings, acting as witnesses to its truth. The verse strongly cautions against corruption and the selling of divine revelation (Allah's verses) for worldly gain or material profit.  Ultimately, upholding Allah's revealed law (the Torah, in this context) is paramount; failure to do so constitutes disbelief (kufr). The overall message emphasizes the importance of adherence to divine law, accountability to God, and the avoidance of worldly temptation when dealing with matters of faith and justice.
orig: إنا أنزلنا التوراة فيها هدى ونور يحكم بها النبيون الذين أسلموا للذين هادوا والربانيون والأحبار بما استحفظوا من كتاب الله وكانوا عليه شهداء فلا تخشوا الناس واخشون ولا تشتروا بآياتي ثمنا قليلا ومن لم يحكم بما أنزل الله فأولئك هم الكافرون

translation: And We prescribed for them in it [the Torah] that life for life, eye for eye, nose for nose, ear for ear, tooth for tooth, and wounds for wounds. Whoever makes amends for it, it is an expiation for him; and whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the wrongdoers.
interpretation: This verse, found in the Quran, discusses the principle of retribution in the context of the Torah. It highlights a system of proportional justice.  The concept of "life for life, eye for eye," etc., is often misunderstood.  It wasn't a call for unrestricted personal vengeance, but rather a codified system to limit retaliatory actions to the equivalent of the harm inflicted.  This was meant to deter excessive retribution and to establish a framework for justice within the society. The verse stresses the importance of following God's revealed laws, emphasizing that those who deviate from these divinely ordained principles of justice become wrongdoers.  Furthermore,  the clause, "Whoever makes amends for it, it is an expiation for him," signifies the possibility of atonement and reconciliation.  A fine or other appropriate compensation, when offered willingly, could serve as a form of penance and release from the prescribed punishment. This underscores the importance of forgiveness and reconciliation in the face of harm or wrongdoing.  It is important to note that this system of retribution was within a specific historical and societal context. The Quran later emphasizes forgiveness and mercy as overarching principles, often transcending literal application of such laws.  These verses, therefore, should be understood within the broader narrative of the Quran's message, emphasizing justice, mercy, and forgiveness as core values that supersede rigid legalistic application in certain specific instances.
orig: وكتبنا عليهم فيها أن النفس بالنفس والعين بالعين والأنف بالأنف والأذن بالأذن والسن بالسن والجروح قصاص فمن تصدق به فهو كفارة له ومن لم يحكم بما أنزل الله فأولئك هم الظالمون
