The subsequent phrases, "He is the Wise, the Knower," underscore the inherent wisdom and knowledge possessed by Allah, implicitly highlighting the perfect order and understanding that governs His creation.  The entire verse serves as a proclamation of Allah's complete ownership and perfect attributes that are acknowledged by all creation, including both the physical and spiritual realms.
orig: الحمد لله الذي له ما في السماوات وما في الأرض وله الحمد في الآخرة وهو الحكيم الخبير

translation: He knows what enters the earth and what comes out of it, and what descends from the sky and what ascends in it.  He is the Most Compassionate, the Most Forgiving.
interpretation: This verse highlights the encompassing knowledge and absolute awareness of Allah (God). It emphasizes that Allah has complete knowledge of everything that happens on Earth, from the subtle processes within the earth's crust to the macroscopic phenomena of plant growth and animal life.  It also encompasses the celestial realm, covering the atmospheric phenomena, the celestial bodies, and even the unseen movements within the heavens.  The verse underscores Allah's perfect knowledge not only of the physical world but also of the spiritual realm, as implied by the encompassing nature of the expression "what ascends in it."  Crucially, this knowledge is coupled with His attributes of mercy and forgiveness, emphasizing that despite His omniscience, He is also merciful and forgiving.  The verse implies that Allah's knowledge extends beyond the human comprehension and intellect, and that He is aware of every detail and aspect of creation.
orig: يعلم ما يلج في الأرض وما يخرج منها وما ينزل من السماء وما يعرج فيها وهو الرحيم الغفور

translation: And those who disbelieved said, "The Hour will not come to us." Say, "Indeed, by my Lord, it will surely come to you.  It is not hidden from the Knower of the unseen, not even the weight of an atom in the heavens or the earth, nor anything smaller than that or larger, except in a manifest book."
interpretation: This verse addresses the denial of the Day of Judgment by disbelievers. It emphatically declares that the Day of Judgment will inevitably occur. The crucial point is that even the most minute or vast aspects of existence are known to Allah, the Knower of the Unseen.  Nothing is hidden from Him, not even the weight of an atom or anything smaller or larger than that.  This is further emphasized by the phrase "except in a manifest book," referring to Allah's knowledge being meticulously recorded and perfectly comprehensive. This demonstrates Allah's absolute control over all events and the impossibility of anything escaping His knowledge and preordained plan for the universe.  The verse thus serves as a strong affirmation of Allah's absolute knowledge and power and a clear warning to those who deny the Day of Judgment. It conveys a message of certainty regarding the inevitable accountability and reckoning that awaits everyone in the hereafter.
orig: وقال الذين كفروا لا تأتينا الساعة قل بلى وربي لتأتينكم عالم الغيب لا يعزب عنه مثقال ذرة في السماوات ولا في الأرض ولا أصغر من ذلك ولا أكبر إلا في كتاب مبين

translation: To reward those who believed and performed righteous deeds; for them is forgiveness and a generous provision.
interpretation: This verse highlights a fundamental principle in Islam: that God rewards those who have faith and act righteously.  It emphasizes that the reward for righteous actions isn't just a worldly one, but also includes forgiveness for past sins and a generous provision in the hereafter.  The concept of 'maghfirah' (forgiveness) is crucial, implying that God forgives the shortcomings and mistakes of those who strive to live a virtuous life.  The 'rizq kareem' (generous provision) signifies a rich reward, encompassing not only material prosperity but also spiritual fulfillment and happiness in the afterlife.  In essence, the verse promises a positive outcome for those who adhere to the Islamic principles of faith and good works.
orig: ليجزي الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات أولئك لهم مغفرة ورزق كريم

translation: And those who strive against Our verses, powerless, for them is a punishment of a painful torment.
interpretation: This verse describes those who actively oppose or deny the signs and revelations of Allah (God) but are ultimately powerless in their efforts.  Their opposition is futile and will be met with a severe and painful punishment.  The "striving against Our verses" could refer to rejecting the message of the Quran, denying its miracles or truth, or actively working to undermine its influence.  The phrase "powerless" emphasizes the futility of their efforts, signifying that Allah's power and truth are insurmountable. The punishment, described as "painful torment", highlights the severity of the consequences for such opposition, emphasizing the importance of submission to Allah's will and acceptance of His revelations.
orig: والذين سعوا في آياتنا معاجزين أولئك لهم عذاب من رجز أليم

translation: And those who are granted knowledge see that which has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth, and it guides to the path of the Exalted, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the role of knowledge and its connection to the truth of the Quran.  It emphasizes that those possessing understanding and insight will recognize the Quran's revelation as true and divinely inspired. This knowledge, in turn, leads one to the righteous path of God, the Exalted and Praiseworthy.  It highlights the Quran's role as a guide to a righteous life. The verse doesn't simply state that the Quran is true, but that those who possess the intellect and ability to contemplate its message will perceive its truth.  The 'Exalted and Praiseworthy' signifies God's supreme status and the beauty and perfection of the path He lays out. It suggests that intellectual and spiritual insight are necessary to truly appreciate the profound message of the Quran.
orig: ويرى الذين أوتوا العلم الذي أنزل إليك من ربك هو الحق ويهدي إلى صراط العزيز الحميد

translation: And those who disbelieved said, 'Shall we show you a man who will inform you, when you have torn everything to pieces, that you are indeed in a new creation?',
interpretation: This verse, from Surah al-Waqi'ah (The Event), highlights the disbelief of those who deny the Day of Resurrection.  They scoff at the idea of a new creation after the destruction of the current world.  The phrase "torn everything to pieces" (مزقتم كل ممزق) signifies the complete disintegration and annihilation of the present order.  The question implies a challenge to the believers, suggesting that if the existing world is destroyed and people are fundamentally changed, it is only to be replaced with more of the same.  They question the concept of a new creation (خلق جديد), specifically in relation to the resurrection and the accountability that follows.  The verse thus portrays the disbelief and the inability of the disbelievers to grasp the divine power capable of such a radical transformation and the subsequent justice of the hereafter.  It underscores the fundamental difference in perspective between the believers, who accept the divine promise of resurrection, and the disbelievers, who deny it and the divine power behind it.
orig: وقال الذين كفروا هل ندلكم على رجل ينبئكم إذا مزقتم كل ممزق إنكم لفي خلق جديد

translation: Do you fabricate a lie against Allah, or does He have a garden [of bliss]? Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in the punishment and the farthest error.
interpretation: This verse, a strong condemnation of disbelief, directly challenges the notion of attributing falsehood to Allah. It essentially says that those who deny the Hereafter are fundamentally mistaken. The "garden" (jannah) mentioned is a metaphor for Paradise. The verse highlights the severe consequences of rejecting the Day of Judgment; the punishment (adhab) and the "farthest error" (dalal al-ba'id) indicate not only a worldly suffering, but a spiritual and eternal one.  It suggests that disbelief in the afterlife is not just a simple difference of opinion, but a misdirection that leads to profound and eternal repercussions. The verse underscores the importance of belief in the ultimate reckoning as a crucial aspect of faith and a decisive factor in one's destiny.
orig: أفترى على الله كذبا أم به جنة بل الذين لا يؤمنون بالآخرة في العذاب والضلال البعيد

translation: Have they not considered what is before them and behind them of the heaven and the earth? If We wished, We could cause the earth to swallow them up, or cause a piece of the sky to fall upon them. Indeed, in that is a sign for every repentant servant.
interpretation: This verse is a powerful reminder of God's immense power and the consequences of ignoring His signs. It addresses those who are disbelieving and have not reflected upon the wonders of creation, both the heavens above and the earth beneath.  The question, "Have they not considered?" is rhetorical. It implies that the evidence of God's power and creation are readily available for observation but are being ignored. The verse highlights the potential for punishment, such as the earth swallowing them or a piece of the sky falling upon them. This is not presented as a direct threat, but as a demonstration of God's absolute control and ability to enforce justice. The phrase "a sign for every repentant servant" emphasizes the importance of reflection and turning back to God. Those who recognize and accept these signs, and therefore repent, will find guidance and meaning in God's creation. The verse serves as a powerful call to contemplation, reflection, and repentance, highlighting the stark contrast between those who observe and reflect, and those who remain oblivious to the wonders and power of God's creation. The imagery also carries a sense of awe and reverence for the Creator's dominion over all things.
orig: أفلم يروا إلى ما بين أيديهم وما خلفهم من السماء والأرض إن نشأ نخسف بهم الأرض أو نسقط عليهم كسفا من السماء إن في ذلك لآية لكل عبد منيب

translation: And We bestowed upon David from Us [a] favor. O mountains, chant praises with him, and [O] birds, and We softened iron for him.
interpretation: This verse highlights the immense favor bestowed upon Prophet David (Dawood) by Allah.  The phrase "We bestowed upon David from Us [a] favor" signifies a comprehensive gift encompassing not only material blessings but also spiritual qualities and divine assistance.  The command to the mountains, birds, and the softening of iron are symbolic acts of submission and service to the Prophet. The mountains and birds, often seen as representing different realms of creation, are metaphorically brought into harmony and service through their association with David. The softening of iron is not just a physical act but also symbolizes the ease and mastery David gained over the natural world through divine power, likely allowing for the creation of tools and weapons for defense and societal advancement.  It suggests a divine power that facilitated David's exceptional abilities. It implies the potential for humanity, when guided by Allah, to master nature and create significant advancements in civilization. The verse demonstrates divine support and highlights the Prophet's unique position in fulfilling God's will on earth.
orig: ولقد آتينا داوود منا فضلا يا جبال أوبي معه والطير وألنا له الحديد

translation: And strive with sincerity and measure in narration, and do good deeds. Indeed, I am Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: This verse encourages a balanced and sincere approach to all actions, particularly communication.  It emphasizes the importance of accuracy and just measure in storytelling and narration.  The call to "do good deeds" (عملوا صالحا) is a universal principle found throughout the Quran, highlighting the importance of ethical conduct and righteousness in all aspects of life. The concluding phrase, "Indeed, I am Seeing of what you do" (إني بما تعملون بصير), emphasizes divine awareness and accountability.  God is aware of all actions, both outwardly visible and the intentions behind them, and individuals will be held accountable for their deeds.  Taken together, the verse calls for a life guided by sincerity, fairness, and good deeds, knowing that God is fully aware and will ultimately judge all actions.
orig: أن اعمل سابغات وقدر في السرد واعملوا صالحا إني بما تعملون بصير

translation: And for Solomon was the wind, its morning journey a month and its return a month.  And We caused to flow for him springs of rain. And of the jinn were some who worked before him by the permission of his Lord. And whoever deviates from Our command, We will make him taste the torment of the blazing fire.
interpretation: This verse highlights Solomon's (peace be upon him) exceptional dominion and the divine blessings bestowed upon him. The wind, a powerful natural force, was subservient to him, capable of traveling vast distances in a month for his errands. This showcases the immense power and control placed in his hands by Allah (God).  The springs of rain were also a unique resource, potentially facilitating agriculture, and indicating Allah's provision in the context of his kingdom. The mention of the jinn working under his command emphasizes the expansive scope of his influence and the myriad of talents available to him.  Furthermore, the verse subtly introduces the concept of accountability and obedience to Allah's commands.  Those who disobeyed were threatened with punishment, illustrating the importance of divine guidance and the consequences of deviation from the prescribed path.  It is crucial to understand that these verses are describing a historical figure, highlighting the divine blessings and powers granted to him according to Islamic tradition, and not advocating for any specific belief in those who believe differently.
orig: ولسليمان الريح غدوها شهر ورواحها شهر وأسلنا له عين القطر ومن الجن من يعمل بين يديه بإذن ربه ومن يزغ منهم عن أمرنا نذقه من عذاب السعير

translation: They make for him (Allah) whatever they wish of mihrabs (prayer niches), statues, basins like [smooth] jars, and firmly set cauldrons.  O House of David, give thanks! And few of My servants are grateful.
interpretation: This verse describes the craftsmanship and artistry of people, specifically highlighting their ability to create various objects for the worship of Allah. The mihrabs, statues, basins, and cauldrons mentioned are not described as idols themselves but rather as examples of human skill and creativity, which should be employed for the glorification of Allah.  The phrase 'They make for him (Allah)' implies that the creation is intended for use in service and devotion to God.  The subsequent injunction, "O House of David, give thanks!" is a reminder of gratitude. It focuses on the importance of appreciating Allah's blessings, including the gifts of talent and skill. The concluding phrase, "And few of My servants are grateful", underscores the reality that true gratitude and appreciation for Allah's gifts are not universal.  The context suggests a possible reference to the Israelites (descendants of David) and their potential for creating exquisite forms of worship and artistic expression as a testament to Allah's power. The message likely encourages both creative expression and a concomitant mindful appreciation for the divine gifts that make such creation possible.
orig: يعملون له ما يشاء من محاريب وتماثيل وجفان كالجواب وقدور راسيات اعملوا آل داوود شكرا وقليل من عبادي الشكور

translation: When We decreed death upon him, nothing but the earthworm revealed his death, consuming his provision.  When he lay prostrate, the jinn realized that if they had known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating punishment.
interpretation: This verse, part of the narrative of Prophet Solomon (Sulayman), highlights the power of divine decree and the limitations of human knowledge, even for those who possess significant worldly power.  It emphasizes the inevitability of death, which even Solomon, with his apparent supernatural abilities, could not escape.  The earthworm, a seemingly insignificant creature, becomes the instrument for revealing his passing, underscoring the humbling nature of mortality.  The jinn's recognition that knowledge of the unseen events would have spared them punishment further emphasizes the futility of trying to defy God's predetermined will.  The verse serves as a reminder of the powerlessness of mankind before the inevitable and the importance of accepting the divine order.  It also suggests that knowledge of the unseen, if it were available, would not eliminate the consequences of certain actions or choices in the afterlife. The punishment is described as "humiliating," suggesting a severe and undeserved suffering.
orig: فلما قضينا عليه الموت ما دلهم على موته إلا دابة الأرض تأكل منسأته فلما خر تبينت الجن أن لو كانوا يعلمون الغيب ما لبثوا في العذاب المهين

translation: Indeed, there was for Saba' in their dwelling-place a sign – two gardens on the right and on the left. [It was said to them], "Eat from the provision of your Lord and be grateful to Him." [It was also said], "A good land and a forgiving Lord."
interpretation: This verse from Surah Saba' highlights the blessings and warnings given to the Sabaean people.  The "gardens on the right and on the left" symbolize the abundance and prosperity bestowed upon them.  The phrase "Eat from the provision of your Lord and be grateful to Him" is a crucial element, emphasizing the importance of gratitude for the blessings received from God. This implies that their prosperity was a gift from Allah, not something earned through their own merit alone.  The mention of "a good land and a forgiving Lord" emphasizes the bounty of the land and the mercy of God.  The Sabaean people were expected to appreciate this, use their resources responsibly, and remain thankful to their Creator.  Ultimately, the verse serves as a reminder of the importance of gratitude and the consequences of neglecting Allah's blessings. It is a cautionary tale, demonstrating how disobedience and ingratitude can lead to punishment, implicitly contrasting the Sabaean's fate with the consequences of those who rejected such divine provision.
orig: لقد كان لسبإ في مسكنهم آية جنتان عن يمين وشمال كلوا من رزق ربكم واشكروا له بلدة طيبة ورب غفور

translation: Then they turned away, so We sent upon them the torrent flood and replaced their gardens with two gardens producing thorny fruit, and some of the thorny lote-tree, little (in amount).
interpretation: This verse recounts the consequences of disobedience and ingratitude.  The people, having been blessed with lush gardens (likely representing prosperity and abundance), rejected divine guidance and refused to acknowledge the blessings.  As a result, God sent a devastating flood that destroyed their paradise.  Instead of the previous abundance, the land yielded only meager substitutes: thorny fruit and limited amounts of the thorny lote-tree.  This highlights the severe punishment that follows defiance of divine will and the ultimate futility of rejecting blessings. The comparison between the original fertile gardens and the barren substitutes underscores the significant loss incurred by turning away from God's guidance.  The "little" thorny lote-tree might suggest that the punishment was proportional to the severity of the transgression. The specific nature of the punishment reflects the nature of their specific disobedience.  It's important to note that the context of this verse is crucial for a full understanding.  It's part of a larger story, likely about a specific community, and the details provided here serve to demonstrate the consequences of their actions.
orig: فأعرضوا فأرسلنا عليهم سيل العرم وبدلناهم بجنتيهم جنتين ذواتي أكل خمط وأثل وشيء من سدر قليل

translation: That is how We recompense them for their disbelief. And do We recompense except the disbelievers?
interpretation: This verse, a direct statement from Allah, describes the divine retribution for disbelief. It states that the recompense (jazainahum) given to those who disbelieve (kafaru) is a fitting punishment for their actions. The second part, "And do We recompense except the disbelievers?" (Wa hal najazi illa al-kafirun), emphasizes that the divine justice system is not arbitrary or selective. It is a fundamental principle of Islamic belief that Allah's justice encompasses all actions, and disbelief warrants a specific response. This verse serves as a reminder of the accountability that awaits those who reject faith, and it highlights the unwavering justice of Allah in His dealings with mankind. The overall implication is that Allah will not leave the disbelievers without a reckoning for their rejection of the truth.
orig: ذلك جزيناهم بما كفروا وهل نجازي إلا الكفور

translation: And We placed between them and the towns which We blessed, manifest towns, and We made the journey therein easy. Travel therein by night and by day, secure.
interpretation: This verse describes a divinely orchestrated arrangement for ease of travel and security.  It speaks of a strategic positioning of settlements (towns) in a way that facilitated safe movement between them.  The phrase "towns which We blessed" likely refers to settlements renowned for their blessings, prosperity, and safety under divine providence.  The "manifest towns" positioned between these blessed settlements made the journey not just easier in terms of distance, but more accessible and safe, offering security both day and night. This concept of ease and security could extend beyond just physical travel, implying a well-ordered system and divinely protected pathways in both the material and perhaps the metaphorical realm. The implication is that God created an environment of security and prosperity, making travel a relatively simple and safe experience for those He favored and who traveled by His design.
orig: وجعلنا بينهم وبين القرى التي باركنا فيها قرى ظاهرة وقدرنا فيها السير سيروا فيها ليالي وأياما آمنين

translation: And they said, "Our Lord, make our journeys far apart, and they wronged themselves. So We made them stories and scattered them utterly. Indeed, in that are signs for every patient and grateful one.
interpretation: This verse describes the fate of those who disobeyed God and their actions had negative consequences.  They prayed for their travels to be prolonged, seeking distance from each other, but this desire was ultimately rooted in their own wrongdoing.  God, in His wisdom, intervened and separated them, making their stories a cautionary example for future generations.  The phrase "scattered them utterly" highlights the complete dispersion and destruction of their community, a fate resulting from their transgression and refusal to learn from their mistakes. The final part emphasizes the importance of observing these divine lessons.  The patient and grateful individuals will find valuable wisdom and lessons in these narratives, recognizing the consequences of wrongdoing and the importance of steadfastness and gratitude towards God's guidance.
orig: فقالوا ربنا باعد بين أسفارنا وظلموا أنفسهم فجعلناهم أحاديث ومزقناهم كل ممزق إن في ذلك لآيات لكل صبار شكور

translation: And indeed, Iblis had truly fulfilled his suspicion against them, so they followed him, except for a party of the believers.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the deception and temptation of Satan (Iblis).  It highlights how Satan's suspicions about the susceptibility of human beings to doubt and disobedience proved accurate. He correctly anticipated that many would be misled and follow his path of disbelief and disobedience. However, the verse also emphasizes the steadfastness of a portion of the believers, who did not succumb to Iblis's temptations.  The verse serves as a reminder of the ongoing struggle between faith and doubt, and the importance of maintaining faith despite the allure of temptation. It also implicitly states that the ultimate choice rests with individuals; Iblis's influence is not absolute, for a righteous group remained steadfast. This is a key concept in the Quran regarding free will and God's testing of humanity.
orig: ولقد صدق عليهم إبليس ظنه فاتبعوه إلا فريقا من المؤمنين

translation: And he had no authority over them except that We might make known who believes in the Hereafter from among them, and who is in doubt concerning it. And your Lord is, over all things, watchful.
interpretation: This verse describes a crucial aspect of divine testing and the role of human free will.  God allows those who disbelieve or waver about the Hereafter to test their faith through trials and challenges.  It emphasizes that the ability of leaders or individuals to influence others is ultimately limited.  Divine sovereignty is paramount; these trials and the resultant actions of those involved serve to reveal and distinguish the faithful from those who are doubtful about the afterlife.  The phrase "He had no authority over them" isn't about powerlessness in the worldly sense but rather about God's absolute control over the outcome and the eventual judgment.  Ultimately, God is aware of everything, and all actions and intentions are under His watchful eye.  The ultimate test of faith is always against the backdrop of the belief in the hereafter, and God is perfectly capable of discerning the sincerity of each individual's belief.
orig: وما كان له عليهم من سلطان إلا لنعلم من يؤمن بالآخرة ممن هو منها في شك وربك على كل شيء حفيظ

translation: Say, 'Call upon those you claim are besides Allah; they possess not the weight of a speck in the heavens or the earth, nor do they have any share therein, and Allah has no need of them, nor they of Him.'
interpretation: This verse, part of a larger discourse, is a powerful refutation of polytheism.  It asserts that the deities worshipped besides Allah possess absolutely no power or influence.  They cannot even affect the smallest particle in the heavens or the earth.  The idea of 'share' (shirk) is emphasized, meaning these entities have no real part in creation or governance.  The verse also underscores Allah's absolute independence and self-sufficiency. He has no need of these imagined entities, and they have no need of Him, making the worship of anything besides Him entirely meaningless and futile.  The imagery of 'the weight of a speck' highlights the insignificance of these idols compared to the vastness and power of Allah.  Essentially, the verse is a declaration that Allah alone is the true and absolute deity, deserving of worship and devoid of any competitors. The use of the imperative 'Say' ('qul') highlights the importance of conveying this truth, challenging the false beliefs of the time and establishing the oneness of God.
orig: قل ادعوا الذين زعمتم من دون الله لا يملكون مثقال ذرة في السماوات ولا في الأرض وما لهم فيهما من شرك وما له منهم من ظهير

translation: And intercession will not benefit with Him except for him whom He has given permission.  So when fear has been removed from their hearts, they will say, "What did your Lord say?" They will say, "The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great."
interpretation: This verse highlights the limitations of intercession in the presence of God.  While intercession can be a valuable aspect of human relationships, it ultimately rests on God's permission and not on human effort alone.  The phrase "except for him whom He has given permission" emphasizes God's absolute sovereignty and control over His judgments. The verse then describes a scene where fear has subsided, and those who previously sought intercession now focus on understanding God's judgment, expressed as "the truth".  The description of God as "the Most High, the Great" underlines His immense power and perfect justice in the divine court of reckoning.  It suggests that the ultimate outcome, the truth, will ultimately stem from and be in accordance with God's absolute authority.  The verse emphasizes that God's judgment is ultimate and any intercession is contingent on His permission. It's a statement of divine sovereignty and the finality of God's decree.
orig: ولا تنفع الشفاعة عنده إلا لمن أذن له حتى إذا فزع عن قلوبهم قالوا ماذا قال ربكم قالوا الحق وهو العلي الكبير

translation: Say, 'Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?' Say, 'Allah.' Indeed, we or you are upon guidance, or in manifest error.
interpretation: This verse is a powerful challenge to those who doubt the divine source of provision. It essentially asks, 'Who is responsible for sustaining you, from the bounty of the heavens and the earth?' The answer, unequivocally, is Allah.  The concluding part of the verse highlights a crucial point about the nature of truth and belief.  The speaker, whether the believer or the disbeliever, implicitly recognizes the existence of a divine order and the reality of guidance.  The statement, "Indeed, we or you are upon guidance, or in manifest error," implies that there is a clear path to truth, and those who stray from it are in obvious misguidance.  The verse acts as a statement of faith and a powerful invitation to reflect on the source of sustenance and the importance of choosing the correct path.
orig: قل من يرزقكم من السماوات والأرض قل الله وإنا أو إياكم لعلى هدى أو في ضلال مبين

translation: Say, "Do not question Us about that which We have transgressed, and do not question Us about what you do."
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Anbiya (The Prophets), emphasizes the divine sovereignty and the limits of human questioning.  It establishes a fundamental principle of the Islamic faith:  God is not obligated to explain His actions or the reasons behind His decrees.  Humans are not entitled to demand answers for God's choices or interventions.  This assertion of God's transcendence affirms His absolute power and wisdom.  Conversely, it also underscores the importance of human accountability.  While God is not obligated to explain, humans are responsible for their actions and will be held accountable for them.  The verse highlights the fundamental difference between the divine realm and the human one, preventing humans from trying to impose their frameworks of understanding on God's. It ultimately calls for acceptance of divine mysteries and an emphasis on the spiritual accountability for our deeds.
orig: قل لا تسألون عما أجرمنا ولا نسأل عما تعملون

translation: Say, 'Our Lord will gather us together, then He will judge between us with truth. He is the Opener, the Knowing One.'
interpretation: This verse, from the Quran, expresses a fundamental Islamic belief about the ultimate judgment by God.  It conveys a message of hope and reassurance for Muslims.  'Say...' (قل) signifies the prophet's role as a messenger conveying divine revelation. The verse affirms that God, the 'Lord,' (ربنا) will eventually gather all humanity (يَجْمَعُ بَيْنَنَا). This gathering refers to the Day of Judgment, a crucial Islamic concept where every soul will be accountable for its actions in life. The phrase 'then He will judge between us with truth' (ثُمَّ يَفْتَحُ بَيْنَنَا بِالْحَقِّ) highlights the fairness and impartiality of God's judgment.  'Truth' (الْحَقِّ) here signifies justice and absolute righteousness. God's judgment will be perfectly just and according to the deeds performed in this life.  The final part, 'He is the Opener, the Knowing One' (هُوَ الْفَتَّاحُ الْعَلِيمُ), attributes two significant qualities to God.  'The Opener' (الْفَتَّاحُ) emphasizes God's ability to reveal and clarify things, to unravel complex issues and ultimately, to open the path to justice. 'The Knowing One' (الْعَلِيمُ) emphasizes God's complete knowledge of all things, past, present, and future, further ensuring the accuracy and fairness of the judgment. The verse thus assures believers that their fate will be determined with absolute justice, that God knows everything, and that the day of judgment will ultimately manifest His perfect knowledge and righteous decree.
orig: قل يجمع بيننا ربنا ثم يفتح بيننا بالحق وهو الفتاح العليم

translation: Say, "Show me those whom you have associated with Him as partners." No, rather, He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: This verse is a powerful refutation of polytheism.  It challenges those who believe in multiple deities to produce evidence of those deities' existence and involvement in the world.  The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is instructed to directly ask the polytheists for proof of their claimed partners to Allah.  The response, "No, rather, He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise," implies the absurdity of such claims.  Allah's absolute power and wisdom are contrasted with the baseless nature of polytheistic beliefs.  It highlights the inherent weakness and lack of logic in associating partners with the one true God, implying that such claims cannot withstand scrutiny and are inherently illogical.  The verse effectively underscores the unparalleled oneness of Allah (Tawhid) and rejects any attempts to diminish His absolute dominion and power.
orig: قل أروني الذين ألحقتم به شركاء كلا بل هو الله العزيز الحكيم

translation: And We have not sent you, [O Muhammad], except as a comprehensive giver of good tidings and a warner, but most of the people do not know.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the universal scope of the Prophet Muhammad's mission.  It declares that the Prophet was sent to all of humanity, not just a particular tribe or nation.  The message encompasses both good news (bashir) and warnings (nadzir).  The 'comprehensive' aspect highlights the all-encompassing nature of the message, covering all aspects of life and belief.  The final clause, "but most of the people do not know," acknowledges the inherent human tendency to resist or ignore divine guidance.  It suggests that the universality of the message doesn't guarantee its acceptance by all, but affirms nonetheless its intended reach and the prophet's role as a messenger to humanity as a whole.
orig: وما أرسلناك إلا كافة للناس بشيرا ونذيرا ولكن أكثر الناس لا يعلمون

translation: And they say, 'When will this promise be, if you are truthful?'
interpretation: This verse reflects a common human response to prophecies or promises, particularly those concerning a future event.  It depicts a skeptical questioning by those who doubt the truthfulness of the prophet and the divine message he carries.  They demand evidence and a demonstration of the promised outcome.  The question implicitly challenges the veracity of the message, implicitly suggesting that if the promise is true, it should already have been fulfilled.  The verse highlights the patience and steadfastness required of prophets and believers in the face of such disbelief and questioning.  The fulfillment of the promise, while ultimately within God's domain and timing, is indirectly related to maintaining faith in God's plan and ultimate justice.  The verse further underscores the importance of believing in divine prophecies despite the apparent delays in their material manifestation. The question implies a potential lack of faith in the messenger or the divine power itself, a test of faith for the believers and the believers' unwavering trust in the plan of God.
orig: ويقولون متى هذا الوعد إن كنتم صادقين

translation: Say, 'For you is an appointed time, a day from which you cannot delay or hasten.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the inevitability and absolute certainty of the Day of Judgment.  It assures believers that this event is fixed and preordained by God, and no human can alter its occurrence.  The phrase 'you cannot delay or hasten' (لا تستأخرون عنه ساعة ولا تستقدمون) highlights the fixed nature of this divine decree.  It's not something that can be anticipated or pushed back, nor can it be rushed.  This understanding underscores the importance of preparing for this day, for it is a crucial aspect of Islamic faith and life, and it signifies the accountability and consequences that come with one's actions in this world.  Essentially, the verse reinforces the belief in the Divine Decree and the absolute control God has over the timing of events, particularly the ultimate judgment of humankind.
orig: قل لكم ميعاد يوم لا تستأخرون عنه ساعة ولا تستقدمون

translation: And those who disbelieved said, 'We will not believe in this Quran, nor in that which was before it.'  And see (O Muhammad), when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord, some of them will turn to others, saying to those who were arrogant: 'Were it not for you, we would have believed.'
interpretation: This verse describes the scene of reckoning on the Day of Judgment.  The disbelievers, refusing to accept the Quran and previous revelations, are now faced with the consequences of their actions.  They witness the stark reality of their choices and the devastating results.  The verse highlights a crucial aspect of human nature: regret.  The verse portrays a profound moment of remorse, where those who were formerly arrogant and resistant now realize the errors of their ways. They acknowledge that the arrogance and disbelief of the arrogant ones (those who refused to believe) hindered them from accepting the truth. This moment of regret, however, is presented as happening *after* the act, highlighting the futility of such belated repentance.  Essentially, the verse paints a powerful image of the Day of Judgement, emphasizing the disbelievers' denial, their eventual remorse, and the consequences of their actions.  It serves as a warning to those who choose disbelief and arrogance, and a reminder of the importance of accepting guidance and truth in this life. Importantly, it also demonstrates that true acceptance and faith should come from within and not be imposed by others.
orig: وقال الذين كفروا لن نؤمن بهذا القرآن ولا بالذي بين يديه ولو ترى إذ الظالمون موقوفون عند ربهم يرجع بعضهم إلى بعض القول يقول الذين استضعفوا للذين استكبروا لولا أنتم لكنا مؤمنين

translation: Those who were arrogant said to those who were weak, "Have we prevented you from guidance after it came to you? No, but you were criminals."
interpretation: This verse, found in the Quran, addresses a specific scenario where a group of people who held positions of power and influence (the 'arrogant') accused a weaker, marginalized group (the 'weak') of being responsible for their own misfortunes and lack of guidance.  The arrogant group essentially claimed that the 'weak' had deviated from the path of righteousness, blaming their supposed failures on the 'weak' themselves. The verse, however, refutes this claim. It declares that the 'weak' were not the cause of their own deviation or misfortune.  Instead, the verse implicitly accuses the arrogant of obstruction and manipulation.  It emphasizes that the truth and guidance (al-hidayah) had indeed been presented, but that the 'arrogant' people were the actual perpetrators of the blocking or the wrongdoers. The 'criminals' here are those who prevented or misrepresented the truth, not the recipients of the message.  This verse is a powerful statement against those who seek to shift blame, and it emphasizes the importance of seeking justice, accountability, and a truthful understanding of events, even in the face of power imbalances and social injustices. It highlights God's absolute awareness of the true motivations and actions of all parties involved, and that ultimately, the responsibility for deviation from the right path lies with those who obstruct it.
orig: قال الذين استكبروا للذين استضعفوا أنحن صددناكم عن الهدى بعد إذ جاءكم بل كنتم مجرمين

translation: And those who were weak said to those who were arrogant, "Indeed, it is the scheme of night and day when you command us to disbelieve in Allah and to make equals to Him." And they concealed repentance when they saw the punishment. And We put shackles on the necks of those who disbelieved. Are they to be recompensed except for what they used to do?
interpretation: This verse describes a confrontation between the weak and the arrogant in the context of a divine message. The weak, acknowledging their vulnerability, accuse the arrogant of misleading them into disbelief in Allah and associating partners with Him.  The command to disbelieve, implied or explicit, is presented as a calculated scheme orchestrated by the arrogance of the disbelievers over a period of night and day.  The key point here is that the arrogant ones are not only misleading but also ultimately controlling. The disbelievers realize the error of their ways only when confronted with the consequences – the punishment, which prompts a clandestine remorse and repentance (not openly expressed). This highlights the hypocrisy and insincerity of their late repentance. Finally, the verse emphasizes the just nature of God's judgment, stating that the disbelievers will only receive the reward or punishment commensurate with their actions.  The mention of shackles further emphasizes the severity of the consequences for those who reject God's guidance.  In essence, the verse underscores the futility of disbelief and the inevitability of divine justice, revealing God's power over time and the consequences of resisting His message.
orig: وقال الذين استضعفوا للذين استكبروا بل مكر الليل والنهار إذ تأمروننا أن نكفر بالله ونجعل له أندادا وأسروا الندامة لما رأوا العذاب وجعلنا الأغلال في أعناق الذين كفروا هل يجزون إلا ما كانوا يعملون

translation: And We sent no warner to any town but its arrogant ones said, "Indeed, we are disbelievers in what you have brought forth."
interpretation: This verse describes a recurring pattern in the stories of the prophets mentioned in the Quran.  It highlights the consistent, predictable, and often arrogant opposition faced by messengers throughout history.  Despite the messengers' warnings, and the clear evidence of truth they brought, the powerful and wealthy elite of the towns they visited consistently rejected the message.  Their rejection wasn't based on reasoned arguments or a lack of understanding, but rather on a refusal to accept that their way of life might need to change.  The 'arrogant ones' (مترفوها)  were often those in positions of power and influence, who prioritized their own comfort, status, and control over the call for righteousness and accountability from God. This pattern underscores the human tendency to resist change and maintain the status quo, even when facing clear evidence of truth.  The verse serves as a reminder to those who come later, that prophets and messengers have faced similar opposition throughout history, and that the message of God remains relevant and challenging to those who cling to the status quo, despite the clear signs and warnings. The verse further emphasizes the resolute nature of God's message and the ultimate consequence of rejecting it. The verse is not about judging the people of the past, but about understanding a recurring human characteristic.
orig: وما أرسلنا في قرية من نذير إلا قال مترفوها إنا بما أرسلتم به كافرون

translation: They said, "We are more in wealth and children, and we will not be punished."
interpretation: This verse describes a common mindset found in many historical and contemporary contexts.  It reflects the attitude of those who judge their value and security primarily by material possessions (wealth) and lineage (children). They are convinced of their invincibility, believing that their superior resources will shield them from any consequences, including divine punishment. This verse highlights the often-erroneous assumption that earthly power and prosperity are guarantees against divine judgment. It serves as a reminder that true strength and security lie not in worldly advantages, but in piety and obedience to God. The verse underscores a fundamental Islamic concept: that earthly possessions and progeny are fleeting and ultimately insignificant in the face of God's judgment.
orig: وقالوا نحن أكثر أموالا وأولادا وما نحن بمعذبين

translation: Say, 'My Lord expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it. But most of the people do not know.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute sovereignty of God (Allah) over provision (rizq).  It affirms that the ability to provide sustenance—be it material wealth, opportunities, or even basic necessities—is entirely within God's control.  He bestows it upon whomever He chooses, without limitation or obligation.  Conversely, He can restrict or withhold provision from anyone He deems appropriate. The key takeaway is that this act of provision is not governed by human actions, merits, or luck, but rather by God's divine will. The verse also subtly criticizes the ignorance of most people who fail to recognize this fundamental truth of Divine sovereignty and often attribute prosperity or hardship to other factors, rather than to the ultimate authority of God.
orig: قل إن ربي يبسط الرزق لمن يشاء ويقدر ولكن أكثر الناس لا يعلمون

translation: Your wealth and your children will not bring you near Us in closeness, except for one who believes and does righteous deeds.  For such, there is a reward of double what they did, and they will be in rooms of safety.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that material possessions and offspring, while valuable in worldly terms, are not the sole criteria for attaining closeness to God.  True closeness and reward are earned through faith (iman) and righteous actions (amal saleh).  Those who possess these qualities will receive a doubled reward for their efforts and will reside in secure, elevated abodes in the hereafter. The emphasis is on the intrinsic value of faith and good deeds,  demonstrating that earthly riches cannot substitute for spiritual striving. The phrase "rooms of safety" (al-gurfāt) is suggestive of a state of peace, security, and comfort in the afterlife, reserved for the righteous. It highlights the ultimate reward for those who dedicate their lives to serving God.
orig: وما أموالكم ولا أولادكم بالتي تقربكم عندنا زلفى إلا من آمن وعمل صالحا فأولئك لهم جزاء الضعف بما عملوا وهم في الغرفات آمنون

translation: And those who strive [against] Our signs, despairing [of success], those will be in the punishment, prepared [to meet it].
interpretation: This verse describes a specific group of people who actively oppose or deny the signs and revelations of God.  They do so with a spirit of hopelessness and despair, seemingly believing their efforts to be futile.  The phrase "strive against our signs" implies a conscious and deliberate attempt to negate, invalidate, or discredit divine messages and evidence.  The crucial element is their *desperation* (معاجزين).  This desperation, instead of leading them to reconsider their position, seems to harden their stance.  The verse signifies that such unrelenting opposition, fueled by despair rather than conviction, will inevitably lead to divine punishment.  This punishment is not merely a threat, but is described as being "prepared" (محضرون), implying a certainty and immediacy about the impending retribution.  In essence, the verse warns against the dangers of resisting clear evidence of God's existence and guidance with a hopeless and ultimately futile mindset.
orig: والذين يسعون في آياتنا معاجزين أولئك في العذاب محضرون

translation: Say, 'My Lord expands provision for whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for whom He wills. And whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it. And He is the best of providers.
interpretation: This verse affirms the absolute power and sovereignty of God in providing sustenance.  It emphasizes that God's provision is not limited by human actions or efforts. He bestows sustenance upon whomever He chooses, in whatever measure He chooses.  This is a key concept in Islamic theology, highlighting the fact that our well-being and prosperity are ultimately in His hands.  The phrase "whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it" underscores God's ability to compensate and care for His creation. It encourages trust in God's plan, reminding believers that any acts of charity or spending, even small ones, will be repaid and replenished by God. Ultimately, it promotes a mindset of reliance on God and a recognition that He is the ultimate provider, the best of providers.  The verse also implicitly addresses the potential anxieties of individuals about the sustenance they need. The message is not just about material provision but about spiritual security and trust in God's plan, regardless of worldly outcomes.
orig: قل إن ربي يبسط الرزق لمن يشاء من عباده ويقدر له وما أنفقتم من شيء فهو يخلفه وهو خير الرازقين

translation: And [the Day] when He will gather them all together, then He will say to the angels, 'Were these the ones you used to worship?'
interpretation: This verse describes a pivotal moment in the Day of Judgment.  On that day, all of humanity will be assembled before God.  God will then address the angels, questioning them about those who were worshipped instead of Him.  The implication is profound.  It highlights the ultimate accountability for false worship and idolatry.  The question itself serves as a stark condemnation of those who turned away from the one true God and sought refuge in other deities.  The verse underscores the importance of worshipping God alone, and the consequences of associating partners with Him. This gathering and questioning serves as a clear demonstration of divine justice and the ultimate triumph of the true faith over false beliefs.
orig: ويوم يحشرهم جميعا ثم يقول للملائكة أهؤلاء إياكم كانوا يعبدون

translation: They said: "Glory be to You, You are our protector against them.  Indeed, they worshipped the jinn, most of them were believers in them."
interpretation: This verse describes a group of people who, in a dialogue likely with a prophet or messenger, acknowledge God's supreme power and protection.  They recognize that their previous worship of jinn (spirits) was a mistake and that God is the true protector against these errant influences.  The phrase "most of them were believers in them" highlights the widespread nature of this false belief within that society. It emphasizes the extent of the deception and the fervent conviction people held in the jinn's power,  suggesting a strong social and cultural influence of the belief system. The verse serves as a testament to the ongoing struggle between true faith and false idols, illustrating that people can be deeply misled and yet still capable of recognizing the truth when presented with it.
orig: قالوا سبحانك أنت ولينا من دونهم بل كانوا يعبدون الجن أكثرهم بهم مؤمنون

translation: So today, none of you will be able to benefit or harm another.  And We will say to those who wronged, "Taste the fire of the Hell which you used to deny."
interpretation: This verse from Surah Al-Zumar (39) describes the final judgment day.  It highlights the absolute separation and accountability that will occur.  The phrase "none of you will be able to benefit or harm another" signifies the cessation of worldly influence and relationships.  Each person will stand solely responsible for their actions, devoid of any ability to intercede or seek assistance from others.  The subsequent statement, "Taste the fire of Hell which you used to deny," emphasizes the reality of divine punishment for those who rejected the message of Allah and His messengers.  This denial, and the associated unjust actions, will now have tangible consequences. The emphasis is on the absolute justice of God, the irreversible nature of the judgment, and the ultimate accountability each individual will face.  The believers who followed the right path will be spared the punishment, while the disbelievers will be held responsible for their past deeds.
orig: فاليوم لا يملك بعضكم لبعض نفعا ولا ضرا ونقول للذين ظلموا ذوقوا عذاب النار التي كنتم بها تكذبون

translation: And when Our clear verses are recited to them, those who disbelieved say: "This is nothing but a man who desires to turn you away from what your fathers used to worship." And they say: "This is nothing but a fabricated falsehood." And those who disbelieved said concerning the truth, when it came to them: "This is nothing but manifest magic.
interpretation: This verse describes the reaction of disbelievers when confronted with the clear and undeniable verses of the Quran.  They reject the message, not out of genuine inquiry, but out of ingrained resistance to change and a desire to uphold the status quo.  They employ various tactics to discredit the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the message.  The disbelievers initially dismiss the Quran as a mere human invention, attempting to portray it as an attempt to lead people away from their ancestral beliefs.  They then label it a fabricated lie.  Ultimately, their rejection escalates to the accusation that it's nothing more than blatant magic.  This indicates a deep-seated denial of the truth presented in the Quran and a refusal to accept divine revelation.  Their arguments aren't based on reasoned debate or a critical examination of the content but rather stem from a defensive posture against the message of the Quran and the potential threat to their established ways of life and beliefs.  The verse highlights the stubbornness and irrationality of those who reject truth when presented with undeniable evidence, choosing instead to cling to their preconceived notions and fears.
orig: وإذا تتلى عليهم آياتنا بينات قالوا ما هذا إلا رجل يريد أن يصدكم عما كان يعبد آباؤكم وقالوا ما هذا إلا إفك مفترى وقال الذين كفروا للحق لما جاءهم إن هذا إلا سحر مبين

translation: And We did not give them any books by which they could study, nor did We send any warner to them before you.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the unique and final nature of the revelation of the Quran to Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).  It asserts that the Quran is a completely new and comprehensive revelation, unlike any previous scriptures (books). The phrase "We did not give them any books by which they could study"  implies that previous prophets and scriptures, while important in their own contexts, did not contain the complete and final guidance that is found in the Quran. The phrase "nor did We send any warner to them before you" stresses the ultimate and unparalleled nature of Prophet Muhammad's prophethood.  It highlights the Quran as the culminating revelation, building upon and surpassing all previous messages, and affirming that no one before Muhammad brought a message comparable to it in scope and completeness. This verse is often used to establish the Quran's unparalleled position as the ultimate guidance for humanity.
orig: وما آتيناهم من كتب يدرسونها وما أرسلنا إليهم قبلك من نذير

translation: And those before them denied [the truth], and they did not attain even a tenth of what We gave them. So they denied My messengers, so how was the reckoning?
interpretation: This verse from Surah al-An'am (The Cattle) serves as a warning to the people of the time of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). It highlights the common pattern of denial and ingratitude that has recurred throughout history. The phrase "those before them" refers to past communities who rejected the prophets and messengers sent to them. Despite the immense blessings and divine guidance they received, these communities failed to appreciate them, and their lack of gratitude resulted in their decline and punishment. The verse emphasizes the severe consequence of rejecting the truth and messengers, alluding to a day of reckoning where those who denied will face the consequences of their actions. The comparison to "a tenth" of the blessings received is a stark contrast. It symbolizes a complete failure to value or benefit from the abundance provided.  The verse underscores the consistent theme in the Quran, emphasizing the importance of gratitude, belief in divine messengers, and the inevitable consequences of disbelief and transgression.  It calls for reflection on this historical pattern and reminds believers to be grateful for the blessings they receive from God and not repeat the mistakes of the past.
orig: وكذب الذين من قبلهم وما بلغوا معشار ما آتيناهم فكذبوا رسلي فكيف كان نكير

translation: Say, "Indeed, I only advise you with one thing: that you stand for Allah, in twos and singly, and then reflect.  There is no paradise for your companion; he is but a warner to you before a severe punishment.
interpretation: This verse urges the believers to dedicate themselves to Allah, emphasizing the importance of individual and collective devotion.  "In twos and singly" highlights the importance of both communal prayer and individual reflection.  It underscores the necessity of consistent remembrance of Allah, whether in prayer with others or in personal contemplation.  The phrase "There is no paradise for your companion" directly addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). It emphasizes that he does not possess the power to grant salvation or paradise.  Instead, he serves as a warner, a messenger bringing a crucial message about the approaching, severe punishment (hellfire) that awaits those who disobey God.  The verse fundamentally stresses the role of the Prophet as a messenger conveying a divine warning, and the ultimate responsibility of the recipients to respond to that warning and to work towards a righteous life in accordance with Allah's commands, highlighting the ultimate responsibility of individuals for their actions and the accountability they face before God.
orig: قل إنما أعظكم بواحدة أن تقوموا لله مثنى وفرادى ثم تتفكروا ما بصاحبكم من جنة إن هو إلا نذير لكم بين يدي عذاب شديد

translation: Say, 'Whatever reward I ask of you, it is for you. My reward is only with Allah, and He is witness over all things.'
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the purely selfless nature of the Prophet's (peace be upon him) mission and the source of his motivation.  He is stating that any perceived reward or gain he might seem to desire from his followers is not personal profit but rather a collective benefit for them.  The true reward, he affirms, lies only with Allah.  The phrase "He is witness over all things" reinforces the absolute knowledge and accountability of Allah, underscoring that everything, including the Prophet's (peace be upon him) actions and intentions, is ultimately under His observation and judgment.  The verse highlights the importance of selfless service and devotion to the divine cause as the sole justification for the Prophet's work, and contrasts that with any earthly, personal gain. This is a powerful statement about the nature of prophecy and the focus on spiritual reward above all else.
orig: قل ما سألتكم من أجر فهو لكم إن أجري إلا على الله وهو على كل شيء شهيد

translation: Say, 'My Lord casts forth truth, the Knower of the unseen,'
interpretation: This verse, a declaration from the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), asserts the absolute truth and authenticity of Allah's revelation.  It highlights Allah's ability to reveal truth in a way that transcends human comprehension.  'My Lord casts forth truth' emphasizes the active and deliberate nature of revelation, not just something discovered passively. The phrase 'the Knower of the unseen' (al-'ālim al-ghāib) underscores Allah's infinite knowledge and understanding of all things, past, present, and future.  The verse asserts that Allah's revelation is not based on human conjecture or guesswork, but rather originates from His perfect knowledge and absolute truth.  It's a powerful statement of the divine origin of the Qur'an and an invitation to trust in its message. The verse implicitly challenges those who doubt the Prophet's message by pointing to the infallible knowledge of the source of that message, Allah Himself.  It also encourages reflection on the vastness of divine knowledge and the limitations of human understanding.
orig: قل إن ربي يقذف بالحق علام الغيوب

translation: Say, 'The truth has come, and falsehood cannot initiate, nor can it return.'
interpretation: This verse asserts the definitive and irrefutable nature of truth (al-haqq).  It declares that truth cannot be created or initiated by falsehood, and that falsehood has no power to bring truth back to its previous state.  In essence, it proclaims the eternal and unassailable victory of truth over falsehood.  The verse implies that any attempts to oppose or replace truth will ultimately be futile and will not succeed. This contrasts falsehood, which is inherently transient and without lasting power.  This concept is central to Islamic belief, emphasizing that truth, revealed by God, is inherent and unchangeable, while falsehood is inherently temporary and cannot endure against it.
orig: قل جاء الحق وما يبدئ الباطل وما يعيد

translation: Say, 'If I have strayed, I have strayed only against myself, and if I have found guidance, it is by what my Lord inspires me. Indeed, He is Hearing, Near.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the individual's responsibility for their own actions and choices.  The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is declaring that any deviation from the right path is a personal failing, a consequence of his own shortcomings. He isn't claiming divine infallibility but acknowledging that guidance comes solely from God.  The phrase 'by what my Lord inspires me' highlights the role of divine revelation in directing the Prophet.  Crucially, the verse also underscores God's attentiveness (hearing) and closeness to His creation, ensuring that divine guidance is always available to those who seek it.  The verse suggests a personal commitment to seeking truth and accountability for one's decisions, but with the underlying understanding that ultimately, guidance comes from God's grace and inspiration.  It is a model of humility and reliance on God's will in the face of the complexities of life.
orig: قل إن ضللت فإنما أضل على نفسي وإن اهتديت فبما يوحي إلي ربي إنه سميع قريب

translation: And if you could see them when they are terrified, and they are being seized from a near place,
interpretation: This verse describes a scene of intense fear and imminent capture.  It vividly portrays the moment of terror when a group is confronted by a threat that is close at hand. The phrase "when they are terrified" ( إذ فزعوا) highlights the overwhelming psychological impact of the impending danger. The phrase "they are being seized from a near place" (وأخذوا من مكان قريب) emphasizes the suddenness and immediacy of the attack.  The implication is that the enemy or force causing the fear is very close, making the situation particularly precarious and alarming.  While the Qur'an doesn't specify the exact historical or metaphorical context for this scene, it evokes a general feeling of helplessness and anxiety in the face of a swift and close assault, likely drawing upon the experience of believers in similar situations.
orig: ولو ترى إذ فزعوا فلا فوت وأخذوا من مكان قريب

translation: And they said, 'We believe in it.' But how could they be brought face-to-face with it, coming from a distant place?
interpretation: This verse, often found in the context of discussions about the prophets and the call to Islam, highlights a common human reaction to a message or belief, particularly one that requires significant effort or sacrifice.  The statement "We believe in it" (آمنا به) expresses a declaration of faith, yet the subsequent question "But how could they be brought face-to-face with it, coming from a distant place?" (وأنى لهم التناوش من مكان بعيد)  indicates a practical, almost skeptical,  doubt.  The "distant place" likely alludes to a geographical distance or more importantly, a significant difference in perspective, beliefs, or lifestyle.  It underscores the internal conflict that can arise when accepting a belief requires substantial change or a challenging journey.  It subtly suggests that true faith isn't merely a verbal affirmation but one that engages with the practical implications of that belief. This highlights the difficulty of embracing new beliefs when they demand a fundamental shift in one's way of life and relationships.  In essence, the verse questions the sincerity of the faith if it is not followed by active engagement and adherence to the call of the belief, especially given the circumstances and obstacles.  The context of the verse is crucial in understanding the specific application of this theme of faith versus action.
orig: وقالوا آمنا به وأنى لهم التناوش من مكان بعيد

translation: And they disbelieved in it before, and they slander the unseen from a distant place.
interpretation: This verse describes a recurring theme in the Quran: the denial and slander of prophets and divine messages by those who oppose them.  "They disbelieved in it before" refers to the past rejection of previous revelations, prophets, or messengers.  The phrase "they slander the unseen from a distant place" highlights the insidious nature of this opposition.  'Unseen' (al-ghayb) refers to the divine and the transcendent, matters beyond human comprehension but known to God. The act of slandering the unseen suggests a malicious intent to undermine the message, likely from a position of perceived superiority or power, potentially from a geographical distance, figuratively representing a detached or arrogant stance.
orig: وقد كفروا به من قبل ويقذفون بالغيب من مكان بعيد

translation: A barrier was placed between them and what they desired, as He did with their predecessors. Indeed, they were in a dubious doubt.
interpretation: This verse describes a divine act of preventing a group of people from achieving their desires.  The phrase "a barrier was placed between them and what they desired" signifies a deliberate obstruction by God.  This obstruction isn't arbitrary; it's a consequence of their prior actions, as the verse states it was similar to what happened to their predecessors.  The phrase "they were in a dubious doubt" highlights the lack of firm faith or commitment to the right path.  The combination of these elements suggests that those who are distanced from God's guidance and favor encounter divine obstacles, ultimately stemming from their own doubts and past misgivings.  Essentially, the verse portrays a consequence-based divine intervention where doubt and lack of faith lead to limitations and a hindering of desires.  The key is not that God prevents good things, but that people's own lack of faith and proper direction create their own barriers.
orig: وحيل بينهم وبين ما يشتهون كما فعل بأشياعهم من قبل إنهم كانوا في شك مريب

translation: Praise be to Allah, the Creator of the heavens and the earth, the One who made the angels messengers with pairs, triplets, and quadruplets of wings. He increases in creation as He wills. Indeed, Allah is over all things powerful.
interpretation: This verse is a declaration of praise and glorification to Allah (God) for His magnificent creation. It highlights His power, wisdom, and unparalleled ability to create and manage everything.  The phrase "the Creator of the heavens and the earth" emphasizes Allah's dominion over the entire universe.  The mention of angels as messengers, with varying numbers of wings, signifies their diverse roles and responsibilities in divine service. The important point is not a specific account of the angels' physical characteristics, but their multiplicity and the vastness of God's creation.  Importantly, the phrase "He increases in creation as He wills" signifies Allah's absolute power and control over His creation. There is no limit to His creative capabilities, demonstrating both the grandeur and complexity of His design. The concluding statement, "Indeed, Allah is over all things powerful," reinforces His absolute authority and mastery over all aspects of existence. In essence, the verse praises Allah for His boundless power and creative capacity, showcased in His vast, complex, and harmonious universe.
orig: الحمد لله فاطر السماوات والأرض جاعل الملائكة رسلا أولي أجنحة مثنى وثلاث ورباع يزيد في الخلق ما يشاء إن الله على كل شيء قدير

translation: Whatever mercy Allah opens for people, there is no one who can withhold it; and whatever He withholds, there is no one who can send it forth after Him. He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's absolute control over His blessings and mercy. It declares that no one can prevent or interfere with the divine grace and favors Allah bestows upon humanity. Conversely, whatever He chooses not to grant, no one can compel Him to bestow. This signifies Allah's absolute sovereignty, power, and wisdom.  It is a powerful reminder that all blessings and hardships ultimately come from Him, and that human efforts are ultimately subservient to His will.  The verse suggests a complete lack of interference or influence from any other power.  The concept of mercy (rahmah) in Islam is paramount, signifying compassion, forgiveness, and guidance.  The verse also highlights the importance of accepting whatever Allah decrees and trusting in His wisdom, even when faced with hardship or disappointment. The phrase "He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise" reinforces the idea that Allah's actions are not arbitrary but are guided by perfect wisdom and power.
orig: ما يفتح الله للناس من رحمة فلا ممسك لها وما يمسك فلا مرسل له من بعده وهو العزيز الحكيم

translation: O mankind, remember Allah's blessings upon you. Is there any creator besides Allah who provides for you from the heavens and the earth? There is no god but He, so how are you deluded?
interpretation: This verse serves as a powerful reminder to humanity of Allah's immense blessings and omnipotence.  It directly challenges the notion of any other creator or provider besides Allah.  The verse highlights the undeniable fact that sustenance, whether from the heavens (rain, etc.) or the earth (crops, etc.), originates from Allah.  By implicitly asking "Is there any other creator?", it asserts Allah's absolute sovereignty and uniqueness in creation and provision. The question "how are you deluded?" is a rhetorical one, rebuking those who may deny or forget these fundamental truths. It's a call to remembrance and reflection on the immense grace and generosity of Allah. The verse is a fundamental theological statement affirming Allah's sole divinity and control over all aspects of creation and sustenance. It's meant to dispel any doubt or misdirection regarding the source of existence and provision.
orig: يا أيها الناس اذكروا نعمت الله عليكم هل من خالق غير الله يرزقكم من السماء والأرض لا إله إلا هو فأنى تؤفكون

translation: And if they deny you, then messengers before you have also been denied. And to Allah do matters return.
interpretation: This verse is a powerful reassurance to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and Muslims in general.  It acknowledges the inherent resistance to prophets and messengers throughout history.  It assures the believers that denying a prophet is not unique to the current time.  Historical precedent demonstrates that this is a common pattern.  Crucially, it emphasizes that ultimately, all matters, including disputes about prophethood, will be resolved and judged by Allah.  The phrase "to Allah do matters return" underscores the ultimate sovereignty of God and His perfect justice. It encourages patience and steadfastness in the face of opposition, reminding believers that Allah's judgment will prevail in the end.
orig: وإن يكذبوك فقد كذبت رسل من قبلك وإلى الله ترجع الأمور

translation: O mankind, the promise of Allah is true. So let not the life of this world deceive you, and do not let the deception of the worldly life deceive you regarding Allah.
interpretation: This verse serves as a crucial reminder to humanity about the ultimate reality of Allah's promises. It emphasizes that Allah's word is absolutely true and certain to be fulfilled.  The verse cautions against being misled by the allurements and temporary pleasures of this worldly life.  The ephemeral nature of worldly possessions and joys is highlighted, reminding us that they are not substitutes for the eternal rewards promised by Allah.  The phrase "do not let the deception of the worldly life deceive you regarding Allah" is key. It warns against allowing worldly pursuits to overshadow our relationship with Allah or to dilute our faith in His justice and eventual judgment.  Ultimately, the verse encourages us to focus on the Hereafter and the true rewards that Allah has promised to the righteous.  Our actions in this world should be guided by faith in the promise of the hereafter and not swayed by the fleeting nature of this life.
orig: يا أيها الناس إن وعد الله حق فلا تغرنكم الحياة الدنيا ولا يغرنكم بالله الغرور

translation: Indeed, Satan is your enemy, so take him as an enemy. He only calls upon his faction to be among the companions of the Blazing Fire.
interpretation: This verse warns against Satan's influence and deceptive tactics.  It clearly establishes Satan as the enemy of humanity.  The verse isn't suggesting a literal enemy in the physical sense, but rather a spiritual adversary who seeks to mislead and corrupt.  Satan's primary method, according to the verse, is to manipulate and entice people into following his deceptive ways.  He calls upon his followers, i.e. those who are susceptible to his temptations, to join him in the eternal punishment of the Blazing Fire (Hellfire). The verse underscores the importance of recognizing and resisting Satan's influence, thus making the choice between right and wrong a conscious one.  It emphasizes that the ultimate outcome depends on our actions and choices, and the danger of blindly following temptation, as it leads to eternal consequences. This verse encourages vigilance against Satan's efforts to mislead individuals away from Allah's guidance and emphasizes the importance of seeking refuge in Allah from the evil of the devil.
orig: إن الشيطان لكم عدو فاتخذوه عدوا إنما يدعو حزبه ليكونوا من أصحاب السعير

translation: For those who disbelieved, there is a severe punishment, and for those who believed and did righteous deeds, there is forgiveness and a great reward.
interpretation: This verse, a common theme throughout the Quran, highlights the fundamental difference between belief and disbelief in the context of divine judgment. It emphasizes the concept of reward and punishment.  Those who reject the message of Islam and its associated righteous actions face a severe punishment in the hereafter. Conversely, those who embrace faith and perform good deeds are promised forgiveness and a generous recompense.  The 'great reward' refers to the ultimate blessings and eternal happiness in Paradise, a profound contrast to the punishment faced by the disbelievers.  The verse underscores the importance of faith and righteous action in the eyes of God, emphasizing the accountability that comes with both choices.  It's a clear statement of God's justice and mercy, revealing that belief and good deeds lead to divine favor and the avoidance of divine retribution.
orig: الذين كفروا لهم عذاب شديد والذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات لهم مغفرة وأجر كبير

translation: So is he whose evil deed is made pleasing to him, so he sees it as good? Indeed, Allah misleads whom He wills and guides whom He wills. So do not let your soul grieve over them out of sorrow. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do.
interpretation: This verse addresses the human tendency to rationalize and justify bad actions.  It highlights that sometimes, individuals may find their wrongdoing appealing and view it as acceptable. This deceptive perception, or the allure of sin, does not absolve them of responsibility.  Allah, in His absolute wisdom and sovereignty, can either lead a person astray or guide them towards the right path.  The verse then cautions against excessive grief or sorrow over the choices of others.  While we should strive to guide and advise, ultimately, responsibility for one's actions lies with the individual.  Our focus should be on our own righteous actions and trusting in Allah's justice and ultimate knowledge of all deeds.
orig: أفمن زين له سوء عمله فرآه حسنا فإن الله يضل من يشاء ويهدي من يشاء فلا تذهب نفسك عليهم حسرات إن الله عليم بما يصنعون

translation: And it is Allah Who sends the winds, raising thereby clouds, and We drive them to a dead land, and thereby revive the earth after its death. Thus is the Resurrection.
interpretation: This verse highlights Allah's power and control over the natural world.  It describes the process of rain clouds being formed and moved by winds to barren lands, leading to the revival and flourishing of the earth. This act of bringing life to a lifeless place mirrors the concept of the Resurrection. Just as the dead land is revived, so too will the dead be resurrected on the Day of Judgment. The verse uses the natural phenomenon of rain to illustrate the far greater miracle of the Resurrection. The imagery conveys a profound message of Allah's power to bring life from death, both in the physical and spiritual realms.  It emphasizes the interconnectedness of all creation and Allah's perfect control over it.  The verse is not merely a description of a natural process, but a parable for a spiritual truth, a sign pointing to the ultimate Resurrection, and a testament to Allah's absolute power over life and death.
orig: والله الذي أرسل الرياح فتثير سحابا فسقناه إلى بلد ميت فأحيينا به الأرض بعد موتها كذلك النشور

translation: Whoever desires dignity, then to Allah belongs all dignity.  Good words and righteous deeds raise one up.  And those who plot evils, for them is a severe punishment.  And their plotting is but failure.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the source and nature of true dignity and success. It asserts that true power and honor originate solely from Allah.  Any individual seeking such elevated status must look to Allah as the source, not themselves or any worldly means.  The verse highlights the importance of virtuous actions, emphasizing that good words and righteous deeds are the means to achieve genuine elevation. These actions are in contrast to the machinations of those who plot evil.  The Qur'an clearly warns that those who engage in deceitful and malicious schemes will face severe punishment.  The final phrase, highlighting the futility of their plots, underscores the eventual failure of those who seek to harm others or undermine divine justice.  It emphasizes that Allah's plan ultimately prevails, and those who seek to oppose it are ultimately defeated, their schemes coming to naught.  In essence, the verse is a call to righteousness, emphasizing the superiority of virtuous conduct over malicious intent. It is a strong reminder that true success and lasting dignity are not found in worldly schemes, but in seeking Allah's pleasure through good deeds and noble conduct.
orig: من كان يريد العزة فلله العزة جميعا إليه يصعد الكلم الطيب والعمل الصالح يرفعه والذين يمكرون السيئات لهم عذاب شديد ومكر أولئك هو يبور

translation: And Allah created you from dust, then from sperm, then made you couples.  And no female bears or lays down except by His knowledge.  And no one lives long or shortens their lifespan except in a Book. Indeed, that is easy for Allah.
interpretation: This verse highlights the profound wisdom and complete control of Allah over creation and human life.  It emphasizes the intricate stages of human creation, beginning with dust, progressing through the development from sperm to the forming of couples.  The verse underscores that every aspect of this intricate biological process, from conception to childbirth, is under Allah's complete knowledge and command.
