It then points to the predetermined nature of life spans, noting that no one lives longer or shorter than what is decreed in the divine record (the Book). This highlights the absolute power and knowledge of Allah, showcasing that even the most minute details of life, from conception to death, are meticulously planned and orchestrated.  The final phrase, 'Indeed, that is easy for Allah,'  underlines His absolute mastery over all things, and that His plan is not hindered by complexity or difficulty.
orig: والله خلقكم من تراب ثم من نطفة ثم جعلكم أزواجا وما تحمل من أنثى ولا تضع إلا بعلمه وما يعمر من معمر ولا ينقص من عمره إلا في كتاب إن ذلك على الله يسير

translation: The two seas are not alike; this one is fresh, palatable and refreshing to drink, and this one is salty, bitter.  From each you eat fresh, tender meat, and you extract ornaments to wear.  And ships are seen sailing through it, to seek its bounty, and that you might give thanks.
interpretation: This verse highlights the diversity and interconnectedness of God's creation, specifically focusing on the contrasting nature of seas.  The fresh, potable water and the salty sea are presented not as separate entities but as parts of a grand system.  Both provide sustenance; the fresh water for drinking and the salty water for the capture of fish, providing nourishment (the "fresh, tender meat") and resources like pearls and other valuables ("ornaments").  The presence of ships navigating these waters emphasizes the practical benefits and resources derived from the seas.  The verse ultimately encourages appreciation and gratitude towards God for these abundant provisions. The "give thanks"  call is crucial; it's not simply about recognizing the bounty but about acknowledging God as the source of that abundance. The verse implies a recognition that the existence of both fresh and saltwater environments, each with its own unique characteristics, is part of a designed and purposeful system created by God.
orig: وما يستوي البحران هذا عذب فرات سائغ شرابه وهذا ملح أجاج ومن كل تأكلون لحما طريا وتستخرجون حلية تلبسونها وترى الفلك فيه مواخر لتبتغوا من فضله ولعلكم تشكرون

translation: He causes the night to enter into the day, and He causes the day to enter into the night. He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running according to a determined time. That is God, your Lord, to Whom belongs the dominion; and those whom you invoke besides Him, possess not even a splinter (of power).
interpretation: This verse highlights the power and sovereignty of God (Allah) over the natural world.  It emphasizes His absolute control over the cyclical nature of day and night, demonstrating His masterful orchestration of the universe. The mention of the sun and moon, both celestial bodies crucial to life on Earth, running according to a specific, divinely ordained timetable, underscores the precision and order inherent in God's creation.  The final part of the verse is a powerful statement of God's exclusive dominion.  It dismisses the concept of any other deities having any power or influence whatsoever, emphasizing that true power and authority belong exclusively to God.  The phrase 'a splinter (of power)' is a powerful metaphorical image, emphasizing the utter insignificance of any supposed divine power other than God's.  The verse serves as a call to monotheism and a reminder of God's comprehensive control over all aspects of existence.  It encourages reflection on the natural world as a testament to God's grandeur and might, and invites the believer to direct their worship solely to Him.
orig: يولج الليل في النهار ويولج النهار في الليل وسخر الشمس والقمر كل يجري لأجل مسمى ذلكم الله ربكم له الملك والذين تدعون من دونه ما يملكون من قطمير

translation: If you call upon them, they will not hear your call. Even if they heard, they would not respond to you. And on the Day of Resurrection, they will deny your associating partners with God. No one can inform you better than a knowledgeable one.
interpretation: This verse highlights the futility of worshipping idols or associating partners with God.  It emphasizes that idols are deaf and dumb, unable to hear or respond to prayers.  Furthermore, it points out the ultimate denial of those who practiced shirk (associating partners with God) on the Day of Judgment.  Their fabricated deities will be of no use to them, and they will be held accountable for their false beliefs.  The statement "No one can inform you better than a knowledgeable one" implies that the Qur'an, revealed by the knowledgeable God, is the ultimate source of guidance and truth regarding this matter of faith and worship.  It also underscores the importance of seeking knowledge and adhering to the divine guidance, as there is no better source of understanding these crucial spiritual issues than God's word.
orig: إن تدعوهم لا يسمعوا دعاءكم ولو سمعوا ما استجابوا لكم ويوم القيامة يكفرون بشرككم ولا ينبئك مثل خبير

translation: O mankind, you are poor in need of God, and God is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the fundamental dependence of humanity on God.  It asserts that humans, in their very nature, are inherently needy and deficient.  We are poor in resources, in knowledge, in understanding, and in the ability to achieve ultimate fulfillment on our own.  Conversely, God is self-sufficient, possessing all perfection and requiring nothing from creation. This inherent difference highlights the crucial role of seeking God's provision, guidance, and grace.  The verse further affirms God's praiseworthiness and inherent goodness, underscoring the proper relationship between the Creator and the created.  It is a reminder that true wealth and fulfillment come from seeking God's favor, not from worldly possessions or achievements.
orig: يا أيها الناس أنتم الفقراء إلى الله والله هو الغني الحميد

translation: If He wills, He will remove you and bring a new creation.
interpretation: This verse highlights God's absolute power and control over all things.  It emphasizes that He is the ultimate creator and sustainer, and that He has the power to replace or remove people, groups, or even entire civilizations if He so chooses.  The verse is not meant to suggest that God will arbitrarily do this, but rather to illustrate His supreme authority and the complete dependence of all creation upon Him.  The "new creation" can be interpreted broadly, signifying a complete transformation, a new era, or a new generation, all ultimately under His will and direction.  It serves as a reminder of God's ultimate power and the temporary nature of worldly existence.
orig: إن يشأ يذهبكم ويأت بخلق جديد

translation: And that is not difficult for Allah.
interpretation: This verse, a common phrase in the Quran, affirms Allah's absolute power and ability.  It emphasizes that nothing is impossible for God.  It often follows a description of a seemingly challenging task or situation, implying that overcoming it is within Allah's effortless capacity.  The verse highlights God's omnipotence and the limitless scope of His power, contrasting it with human limitations.  It serves as a reassurance and a reminder that God has complete control over all things, and nothing is beyond His reach or power to achieve.
orig: وما ذلك على الله بعزيز

translation: No bearer of burden will bear the burden of another. And if one who is burdened calls upon another to share his burden, not even a bit of it will be carried by the other, even if he is a close relative. Indeed, you are only a warner to those who fear their Lord unseen, and establish prayer. And whoever purifies himself, purifies himself only for his own sake. And to Allah is the final destination.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the individual's accountability for their own actions.  It states unequivocally that no one can bear the sins or burdens of another, not even a close relative. This highlights the crucial concept of personal responsibility in Islam.  The individual's actions, good or bad, have direct consequences for themselves alone.  The verse further emphasizes the role of the Prophet (peace be upon him) as a warner.  He is tasked with conveying the message of God's warnings and the importance of piety and prayer to those who are receptive.  The verse also touches upon the concept of self-purification ('ittakah').  The act of purifying oneself is solely for one's own spiritual benefit and growth, and ultimately, all individuals return to Allah for judgment and accountability.
orig: ولا تزر وازرة وزر أخرى وإن تدع مثقلة إلى حملها لا يحمل منه شيء ولو كان ذا قربى إنما تنذر الذين يخشون ربهم بالغيب وأقاموا الصلاة ومن تزكى فإنما يتزكى لنفسه وإلى الله المصير

translation: The blind person and the one who sees are not equal.
interpretation: This verse highlights the fundamental difference between those who possess the capacity for understanding and insight (the "seeing") and those who lack it (the "blind").  It emphasizes the importance of knowledge, wisdom, and understanding in matters of faith and life.  It implies a clear distinction between those who are guided by reason and truth and those who are not.  The verse isn't necessarily a condemnation of blindness in a literal sense, but rather an allegorical expression. It represents the contrast between spiritual awareness and spiritual ignorance, between those who grasp divine guidance and those who do not.  Ultimately, it points to the unequal rewards and consequences of accepting or rejecting divine knowledge and guidance, highlighting the importance of seeking truth and understanding for a fruitful and righteous life.
orig: وما يستوي الأعمى والبصير

translation: Neither darkness nor light
interpretation: This verse, taken in isolation, is quite abstract.  It doesn't describe a specific event or situation.  It emphasizes the absence of a definitive, exclusive choice between two extremes.  A possible interpretation might be a statement about the limitations of human perception of reality.  The duality of light and darkness, often representing good and evil, knowledge and ignorance, or even life and death, is negated.  This negation could point to the transcendence of God beyond human categories or the illusory nature of those dichotomies, that things aren't always simply one or the other.  However, without context from the surrounding verses, the precise meaning remains open to various interpretations within the broader theological framework of the Qur'an.
orig: ولا الظلمات ولا النور

translation: Neither the shade nor the heat
interpretation: This verse, taken in isolation, likely refers to a state of discomfort or hardship.  It suggests a lack of respite or relief from both the oppressive heat and the meager comfort a shadow might offer.  The absence of both extremes implies a harsh, unforgiving environment.  Without further context within the surrounding verses, a precise interpretation is difficult, but it could apply to various situations, from physical hardship to spiritual emptiness or a lack of support. It highlights the difficulty of enduring challenging circumstances where neither conventional comfort nor protection is available.   The Qur'an often uses imagery to convey deeper meanings, and understanding the context is vital to gaining a more complete understanding.
orig: ولا الظل ولا الحرور

translation: The living and the dead are not equal. Indeed, God hears whom He wills, and you are not able to hear those in the graves.
interpretation: This verse highlights the fundamental difference between the living and the dead, emphasizing that God possesses a unique and absolute power of hearing that extends beyond human comprehension.  It stresses the limited capacity of humans to perceive or understand the realm of the deceased.  The verse suggests that while we might hear the words and actions of the living, we cannot communicate with or hear those in the graves.  This emphasizes God's absolute knowledge and control over all things, including the unseen realms and the realm of the dead. The verse also hints at the ultimate judgment that awaits all individuals, where God's hearing and understanding will encompass both the living and the dead, judging them according to their deeds.
orig: وما يستوي الأحياء ولا الأموات إن الله يسمع من يشاء وما أنت بمسمع من في القبور

translation: Indeed, you are only a warner.
interpretation: This verse, found in several chapters of the Quran, is a common message to the prophets and messengers. It emphasizes their role as a warning or a herald of the impending consequences of disbelief and disobedience.  It's not about their ability to compel belief or force action, but rather their duty to deliver the message of Allah (God).  The verse underscores the fundamental truth that humans are ultimately responsible for their choices, and the prophets are merely vehicles for conveying divine warnings.  They are not omnipotent; their power lies in delivering the message, and the recipients bear the responsibility of responding to it.  The ultimate reward or punishment, therefore, is dependent on individual actions, not the prophets' efforts to change them directly.
orig: إن أنت إلا نذير

translation: Indeed, We have sent you, [O Muhammad], with the truth, as a bringer of good tidings and a warner. And there is no nation but that a warner has passed through it.
interpretation: This verse establishes the universality of prophethood and the responsibility of prophets to deliver messages of good news and warning to all people.  It emphasizes that no community or nation has been left without receiving a message from a prophet, reminding them of God's guidance and the consequences of disobeying it.  The phrase "with the truth" highlights the divine origin and authenticity of the message brought by the Prophet Muhammad. The verse serves as a foundational concept in Islamic theology, underpinning the belief that God's message is universal and that no one is excused from receiving and considering it. The implication is that every person has a chance to accept God's guidance and avoid the penalties described in the warning component of the message.
orig: إنا أرسلناك بالحق بشيرا ونذيرا وإن من أمة إلا خلا فيها نذير

translation: And if they deny you, then indeed those before them denied [their messengers], when their messengers came to them with clear proofs, and with scriptures and the illuminating Book.
interpretation: This verse is a powerful rebuttal to those who might reject the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). It asserts that denial of prophethood is not unique to his time.  Throughout history, previous prophets and messengers also faced similar rejection from their communities.  The phrase "clear proofs" (al-bayyināt) emphasizes the undeniable evidence, miracles, and signs that accompany true prophets.  "Scriptures" (al-zubur) and "the illuminating Book" (al-kitāb al-munir) refer to the revealed scriptures of the prophets prior to Muhammad (peace be upon him), including the Torah and the Gospel, which all point to the ultimate truth. The verse highlights the recurring theme of denial throughout history and reinforces the message that the rejection of a prophet is a repeated pattern, a testament to the common human tendency to resist divine revelation,  making the current denial of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) a part of a larger, historical reality.  The verse is meant to strengthen the Prophet and his followers' resolve in the face of opposition by reminding them of the universality of this experience.
orig: وإن يكذبوك فقد كذب الذين من قبلهم جاءتهم رسلهم بالبينات وبالزبر وبالكتاب المنير

translation: Then she seized those who disbelieved. So how was the questioning?
interpretation: This verse, while seemingly isolated, likely refers to the Day of Judgement and the punishment of the disbelievers.  The phrase "Then she seized those who disbelieved" alludes to divine retribution.  'She' likely refers to God or to a manifestation of divine power.  The act of seizing suggests a forceful and decisive capture, implying a swift and inevitable judgment for those who rejected faith. The question "So how was the questioning?" (or 'So how was the reckoning?') emphasizes the severity and finality of the divine interrogation. It highlights the utter unpreparedness and lack of defense the disbelievers will face, emphasizing the profound and unforgettable nature of their confrontation with God's judgment on the Day of Judgment. The exact nature of the questioning and its consequences are left to the divine domain, prompting reflection on the importance of faith and submission to God's will.
orig: ثم أخذت الذين كفروا فكيف كان نكير

translation: Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky, and thereby brings forth fruits of diverse colours? And from the mountains, [springs forth] vegetation, white and red, of varying colours, and black ravens.
interpretation: This verse is a powerful reminder of Allah's artistry and power in creation.  It highlights the interconnectedness of natural elements, showing how water, a fundamental element, facilitates the growth of diverse fruits and vegetation.  The description of the varying colours of fruits emphasizes the beauty and abundance of creation.  The mention of the different colours of the mountains' vegetation, including white and red, further showcases the vastness of Allah's creation and the intricate details within it.  The inclusion of black ravens further underlines the diversity found in creation, showcasing different forms and colours of life, all orchestrated by Allah.  The verse serves as a testament to the divine origin and perfection of creation.  It invites contemplation of the beauty and order in the world around us, acknowledging Allah's profound and encompassing power.
orig: ألم تر أن الله أنزل من السماء ماء فأخرجنا به ثمرات مختلفا ألوانها ومن الجبال جدد بيض وحمر مختلف ألوانها وغرابيب سود

translation: And of mankind, and of cattle, and of the grazing animals, are diverse colors. Thus, it is only the knowledgeable among His servants who fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Exalted in Might, Forgiving.
interpretation: This verse highlights the diversity of creation, emphasizing that the variety of colors found in humans, animals, and livestock is a sign of Allah's artistry and power.  Importantly, it links this diversity to a crucial point:  the fear of Allah is not a characteristic shared by all, but rather reserved for those who possess knowledge (علماء).  The verse suggests that true understanding and knowledge of Allah leads to a deeper reverence and fear of Him, a fear stemming not from blind awe, but from a conscious appreciation for the divine artistry and wisdom behind creation.  The verse also asserts Allah's power and forgiveness, implying that those who develop this fear through knowledge are ultimately assured of His mercy.  In essence, the verse promotes the pursuit of knowledge as a path to a deeper relationship with the divine, contrasted with a simple, unthinking fear or reverence.  It's not merely the *visual* diversity that's important, but the *intellectual* diversity of understanding that's crucial to encountering and respecting the divine will.
orig: ومن الناس والدواب والأنعام مختلف ألوانه كذلك إنما يخشى الله من عباده العلماء إن الله عزيز غفور

translation: Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah, establish prayer, and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly, hope for a trade that will not be lost.
interpretation: This verse praises those who diligently study and reflect upon the Quran (the Book of Allah), who uphold the prescribed prayers (Salah), and who generously donate their wealth, both openly and discreetly.  The phrase "a trade that will not be lost" signifies a transaction that yields eternal rewards.  The verse highlights the importance of piety in all its forms, linking the act of reading and reflecting on the divine text, consistent prayer, and charitable giving as integral components of a righteous life.  These actions, performed with sincerity and devotion, are not merely earthly transactions but rather investments in an enduring, invaluable reward in the hereafter.  The secret and open acts of charity emphasize the spirit of generosity and the importance of consistency in acts of worship, underscoring the believer's complete devotion to God and their desire for His pleasure, rather than worldly gain.  The phrase "trade that will not be lost" implies that the benefits of these actions are secure, permanent, and superior to any earthly gain, contrasting with earthly possessions that may be lost or consumed. This verse encourages believers to prioritize these actions over fleeting worldly pursuits, as these deeds are the surest path to lasting happiness and success in the afterlife.
orig: إن الذين يتلون كتاب الله وأقاموا الصلاة وأنفقوا مما رزقناهم سرا وعلانية يرجون تجارة لن تبور

translation: That He may fulfill their rewards and increase them from His bounty. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Thankful.
interpretation: This verse, often found in the context of rewards for righteous deeds, emphasizes the generosity and fulfillment of Allah (God). It states that Allah will not only grant the promised rewards to those who have done good, but will also enhance those rewards with further blessings from His abundance.  The phrase "fulfill their rewards" highlights the principle of justice and recompense in Islam.  Allah's bounty goes beyond mere compensation; it entails an increase, a gracious enrichment beyond what was initially deserved.  The concluding part, "Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Thankful," serves as a reminder of Allah's attributes.  His forgiveness underscores the fact that even if individuals have fallen short, His generosity is limitless, and His thankfulness indicates that He appreciates the efforts of His creation.  This verse, therefore, promises not only just recompense but also abundant blessings and acts as a powerful motivator for good deeds, recognizing that the rewards extend far beyond our limited understanding of merit.
orig: ليوفيهم أجورهم ويزيدهم من فضله إنه غفور شكور

translation: And that which We have revealed to you of the Book is the truth, confirming that which is before it. Indeed, Allah is Ever-Knowing of His servants, and Ever-Seeing.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the divine origin and the truthfulness of the Quran.  It states that the Quran is a continuation and confirmation of the previous scriptures (like the Torah and the Gospel).  The phrase "that which is before it" (mā bayna yadayhi) refers to the earlier revelations.  The verse asserts that the Quran is not a new religion but a culmination and refinement of the message of the one true God.  Crucially, it emphasizes Allah's omniscience and omnipresence, stating He is fully aware of and observant of His creation. This knowing and seeing is not just about what we do, but also about our inner thoughts and intentions.  Ultimately, this verse establishes the Quran as a divinely revealed and truthful book, and implicitly asserts the consistent, unified message of God throughout history.  It also highlights the ultimate responsibility of humanity before an all-knowing and all-seeing God.
orig: والذي أوحينا إليك من الكتاب هو الحق مصدقا لما بين يديه إن الله بعباده لخبير بصير

translation: Then We bequeathed the Book to those whom We chose from among Our servants. Among them is one who is unjust to himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who hastens in good deeds by Allah's permission. That is the great favor.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the diverse responses and actions of those chosen by God. The "Book," in this context, refers to the Quran, or perhaps more broadly to divine guidance and knowledge.  God chose certain individuals, presumably prophets and righteous people, to receive and transmit this knowledge.  The verse then highlights the varying degrees of human response to this knowledge and responsibility.  Some are "unjust to themselves," perhaps failing to live up to the standards revealed. This could indicate those who knowingly sin or neglect their duty. Others are "moderate," showing balance and righteousness in their lives.  Finally, some are "hastening in good deeds by Allah's permission." These individuals demonstrate proactive piety, acting with diligence and complete submission to God's will.  The verse ultimately emphasizes the profound favor bestowed upon those chosen for this role, not only through the gift of the Book, but also through the vast range of potential responses within their lives. It underscores that the path of faith is a spectrum, encompassing striving for excellence and acknowledging that individual journeys vary. Ultimately, striving for good is the goal, regardless of individual circumstances and progress.
orig: ثم أورثنا الكتاب الذين اصطفينا من عبادنا فمنهم ظالم لنفسه ومنهم مقتصد ومنهم سابق بالخيرات بإذن الله ذلك هو الفضل الكبير

translation: They will enter Gardens of Eden, adorned with bracelets of gold and pearls. Their garments there will be of silk.
interpretation: This verse describes the luxurious and exquisite rewards awaiting the believers in Paradise.  The imagery of "Gardens of Eden" evokes a place of beauty, tranquility, and abundance.  The mention of "bracelets of gold and pearls" symbolizes immense wealth, prestige, and exquisite adornment.  The "silk" garments further highlight the opulence and comfort of Paradise, emphasizing the surpassing excellence of this afterlife reward compared to worldly pleasures.  The verse paints a picture of heavenly splendor and lavish rewards for righteous deeds, showcasing the divine generosity and magnificence of Allah.
orig: جنات عدن يدخلونها يحلون فيها من أساور من ذهب ولؤلؤا ولباسهم فيها حرير

translation: And they said: "Praise be to Allah who has removed from us grief. Indeed, our Lord is Forgiving, Thankful.
interpretation: This verse expresses the gratitude of a group of people who have experienced a period of sadness or hardship.  They acknowledge Allah's role in alleviating their suffering.  The phrase "removed from us grief" signifies the alleviation of sorrow, distress, or any form of affliction.  "Forgiving" (Ghafur) and "Thankful" (Shakur) are attributes of Allah that highlight His mercy, compassion, and appreciation for the supplications of His creation.  The verse reflects a profound sense of thankfulness and trust in Allah's ability to ease burdens and grant relief.  It's a testament to the belief that Allah is the ultimate source of comfort and support during times of adversity and that expressing gratitude for His blessings is a vital component of faith.
orig: وقالوا الحمد لله الذي أذهب عنا الحزن إن ربنا لغفور شكور

translation: The One who has granted us the abode of permanence by His grace; no hardship or weariness shall touch us there.
interpretation: This verse expresses gratitude for a state of lasting comfort and ease, free from hardship and toil. It speaks of a dwelling place (dar al-maqama) that is a gift from God, implying a paradise or a state of eternal bliss.  The phrase "no hardship or weariness shall touch us there" directly counters the difficulties and trials of this earthly life.  The verse likely refers to the eternal abode (Jannah), promised to those who believe and follow God's path, highlighting the immeasurable grace and provision of God in granting such a blissful state. It emphasizes the complete absence of suffering and the profound peace found in the afterlife, a reward for righteous living in this world.
orig: الذي أحلنا دار المقامة من فضله لا يمسنا فيها نصب ولا يمسنا فيها لغوب

translation: And those who disbelieved, for them is the Fire of Hell. They will not be decreed upon to die, nor will their torment be lightened. Thus do We recompense every disbeliever.
interpretation: This verse describes the eternal and inescapable punishment awaiting those who reject faith in Islam.  The phrase "they will not be decreed upon to die" signifies a continuous, unending torment.  It emphasizes the permanence of the punishment for disbelief.  The mention of the torment not being lightened further highlights the severity and unrelenting nature of the punishment. It is a consequence, not a temporary trial. The final part of the verse, "Thus do We recompense every disbeliever," establishes a clear causal link between disbelief and the decreed punishment.  It signifies a just divine judgment, and a fundamental principle of reward and retribution in the afterlife.  The imagery of Hellfire here is not meant to be taken literally as a physical place, but rather a metaphor for the consequences of rejecting God's guidance and the ultimate separation from divine mercy.  This verse is a powerful statement of Islamic eschatology and emphasizes the importance of faith and submission to God's will.
orig: والذين كفروا لهم نار جهنم لا يقضى عليهم فيموتوا ولا يخفف عنهم من عذابها كذلك نجزي كل كفور

translation: And they will cry out within it, "Our Lord, bring us out so that we may perform righteous deeds other than those which we used to perform. Were We not granted a lifetime in which those who would remember, remember?  And a warner came to you, so taste what you have earned, and for the wrongdoers, there is no helper.
interpretation: This verse describes the scene of the Day of Judgment, where the disbelievers, having lived their lives and now facing the consequences of their actions, will desperately plead with God for a chance to do good.  Their plea highlights a fundamental truth about human life—that a period of life was given to them for reflection and righteous action, but they wasted it.  The presence of a messenger (the warner) is also emphasized, underscoring the fact that they were warned and given the opportunity to choose the right path.  The verse further emphasizes the concept of accountability and the inevitable consequences of wrongdoing, stating that the wrongdoers will not find any help or support on that day.  The phrase "taste what you have earned" signifies that they will experience the full weight of their actions and the results of their choices. The emphasis on wasted time further reinforces the importance of utilizing life's opportunities for good deeds, underscoring the transient nature of life and the ultimate judgment that awaits all people.
orig: وهم يصطرخون فيها ربنا أخرجنا نعمل صالحا غير الذي كنا نعمل أولم نعمركم ما يتذكر فيه من تذكر وجاءكم النذير فذوقوا فما للظالمين من نصير

translation: Indeed, Allah is Knowing of the unseen of the heavens and the earth. Indeed, He is Knowing of the inner selves.
interpretation: This verse highlights Allah's comprehensive knowledge. It affirms that He is fully aware of everything unseen, encompassing both the heavens and the earth.  This includes all hidden things and events.  Furthermore, the verse emphasizes Allah's knowledge of the innermost thoughts and intentions of people.  This intimate knowledge extends beyond observable actions and delves into the hidden recesses of the human heart, implying that nothing is concealed from His awareness.  The verse underscores the vastness of divine knowledge and emphasizes that Allah is not limited in His understanding, a concept crucial to Islamic theology.
orig: إن الله عالم غيب السماوات والأرض إنه عليم بذات الصدور

translation: He is the One who made you successors upon the earth. So whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief. And the disbelievers will not increase their disbelief in the sight of their Lord except with aversion, and the disbelievers will not increase their disbelief except with loss.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the crucial role humans play as successors (khalīfah) on Earth, entrusted with responsibility and stewardship.  It asserts that those who reject this trust and choose disbelief (kufr) will bear the consequences of their actions.  Crucially, the verse highlights that disbelief doesn't just stay static; it doesn't simply remain a personal matter.  Rather, it results in increased aversion from God (maqta).   Furthermore, it implies a direct correlation between disbelief and loss (khsara).  This loss isn't simply material; it encompasses spiritual, moral, and eventual consequences in the hereafter.  The verse underscores the inherent accountability that comes with this position of trust.  It doesn't describe disbelief as inevitable, but rather as a choice with repercussions, implying that one's rejection of God's guidance leads to a deepening isolation from His blessings and ultimately, greater loss in the Divine Court.
orig: هو الذي جعلكم خلائف في الأرض فمن كفر فعليه كفره ولا يزيد الكافرين كفرهم عند ربهم إلا مقتا ولا يزيد الكافرين كفرهم إلا خسارا

translation: Say, "Look at your partners whom you invoke besides Allah. Show me what they have created from the earth, or do they have a share in the heavens? Or have We given them a Book, so that they are clear about it?" Rather, the wrongdoers only delude one another with delusion.
interpretation: This verse is a powerful challenge to those who believe in partners to God (shirk). It directly confronts their claims of divinity for other entities, by asking for tangible evidence of their creation.  It highlights the absurdity of such claims, pointing out the lack of any tangible contribution to the universe or any divinely revealed scripture from these supposed partners.  The verse emphasizes that the wrongdoers (those who ascribe partners to God) only deceive each other with empty promises and illusions, leading themselves and others astray.  The message is clear: Allah alone is the Creator and Sustainer, and there is no evidence for any other deity.  The verse reinforces the Quran's core message of Tawhid (the oneness of God) and the futility of polytheistic beliefs. It underscores the responsibility of the believers to reject all forms of shirk and to seek knowledge and evidence in matters of faith.
orig: قل أرأيتم شركاءكم الذين تدعون من دون الله أروني ماذا خلقوا من الأرض أم لهم شرك في السماوات أم آتيناهم كتابا فهم على بينت منه بل إن يعد الظالمون بعضهم بعضا إلا غرورا

translation: Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth from collapsing. And if they were to collapse, no one, after Him, would hold them. Indeed, He is Kind and Forgiving.
interpretation: This verse asserts the absolute power and control of Allah over the universe.  It emphasizes that the heavens and the earth are sustained by His will and power alone, and that no other being or force could maintain their existence if Allah were to remove His sustaining hand.  The concluding phrase, "Indeed, He is Kind and Forgiving," highlights the contrast between Allah's absolute power and His merciful nature.  While His power prevents the destruction of the universe, His inherent kindness and forgiveness are attributes that shape His relationship with creation.  It's a powerful statement about the omnipotence and inherent benevolence of God, highlighting that His power is not exercised in a capricious manner, but within a framework of mercy and forbearance.
orig: إن الله يمسك السماوات والأرض أن تزولا ولئن زالتا إن أمسكهما من أحد من بعده إنه كان حليما غفورا

translation: And they swore by Allah, the utmost of their oaths, that if a warner came to them, they would surely be more guided than any other nation. But when a warner came to them, it only increased their aversion.
interpretation: This verse describes a common human response to prophets and messengers.  It highlights the hypocrisy of a people who outwardly pledge belief and promise to follow the guidance of a prophet, but inwardly reject that guidance when it actually arrives.  They claim they would be the most righteous of people if a prophet were sent, effectively boasting of their potential virtue.  However, upon the actual arrival of the warner – the prophet – they show nothing but opposition, resistance, and aversion to the message.  The verse underscores the human tendency to resist change, even when that change promises betterment. The promise of righteousness is often made with the tongue but not truly embraced with the heart.  Instead of accepting the message and seeking guidance, their pride and self-sufficiency lead them to rejection.  This is a recurring theme in the Quran, highlighting the danger of empty promises and the importance of genuine acceptance of the divine message. Ultimately, the verse serves as a warning against such deception, encouraging reflection on one's true intentions and sincerity of belief.
orig: وأقسموا بالله جهد أيمانهم لئن جاءهم نذير ليكونن أهدى من إحدى الأمم فلما جاءهم نذير ما زادهم إلا نفورا

translation: By arrogance on earth and by evil scheming. Evil scheming does not encircle except its people. So do they await except the precedent of the former? You will not find for the decree of Allah any change, and you will not find for the decree of Allah any alteration.
interpretation: This verse warns against arrogance and harmful plotting on earth.  It emphasizes that such actions will ultimately backfire on those who perpetrate them, as the consequences will inevitably befall them. The phrase "the precedent of the former" refers to the fates of past communities who engaged in similar behavior.  The verse highlights the unchanging and unalterable nature of Allah's decrees.  It serves as a reminder that those who act unjustly or arrogantly will face the consequences, while those who submit to Allah's judgment will find His justice. It underscores the importance of adhering to divine principles and avoiding human ambition that transcends the bounds of the divine order.  Ultimately, it is a call to reflection and a lesson on the futility of defying Allah's established laws.
orig: استكبارا في الأرض ومكر السيئ ولا يحيق المكر السيئ إلا بأهله فهل ينظرون إلا سنت الأولين فلن تجد لسنت الله تبديلا ولن تجد لسنت الله تحويلا

translation: Have they not traveled through the land, observing the fate of those who came before them? They were stronger than them in power, yet Allah did not deprive them of anything in the heavens or on the earth. Indeed, He is Knowing and Powerful.
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical question, challenging those who are disbelieving or heedless to reflect on history.  It urges them to look at the examples of past communities, particularly those who were more powerful than their current generation.  The verse highlights that even those powerful communities faced consequences for their actions and ultimately met their demise. This is a reminder that Allah's power extends over all things, in both the unseen and seen realms. He is aware of everything, and possesses absolute power over all circumstances, rewarding and punishing as He deems fit. The verse underscores that strength and power are ultimately transient, while Allah's judgment is permanent and just.  It is a cautionary tale, urging reflection and adherence to Allah's guidance, instead of relying on worldly power alone.
orig: أولم يسيروا في الأرض فينظروا كيف كان عاقبة الذين من قبلهم وكانوا أشد منهم قوة وما كان الله ليعجزه من شيء في السماوات ولا في الأرض إنه كان عليما قديرا

translation: If Allah were to hold people accountable for their deeds, He would not leave a single beast upon the earth. But He postpones them to a specified time. So when their time comes, Allah is indeed Seeing of His servants.
interpretation: This verse addresses the seemingly disparate treatment of humans and animals, and the concept of divine justice and the appointed time (al-ajal).  It emphasizes that Allah is not arbitrary in His dealings.  If He were to immediately punish humans for all their deeds, the earth would be devoid of life, including animals.  Instead, He allows a period for humans to make choices and earn rewards or bear consequences, holding back punishment until a predetermined time.  The key point is that Allah is aware of everything His servants do; He sees their actions, their intentions, and their ultimate fate.  The verse thus highlights the balance and fairness in divine justice, the grace and mercy of God in allowing time for repentance, and God's omnipotence and constant awareness of His creation.
orig: ولو يؤاخذ الله الناس بما كسبوا ما ترك على ظهرها من دابة ولكن يؤخرهم إلى أجل مسمى فإذا جاء أجلهم فإن الله كان بعباده بصيرا

translation: Yā Sīn.
interpretation: This verse, "Yā Sīn," is a surah (chapter) title, not a complete verse in the traditional sense.  It is the name of the chapter, and is often recited as a way of invoking God's blessings and seeking His guidance.  The meaning derives not from a literal translation, but rather from the overall context and thematic concerns of the chapter. The letter "Yā" is a vocative particle calling on God's attention, "Sīn" is a letter in the Arabic alphabet,  and its significance is thought by some scholars to be related to the numerous miracles and signs in the Qur'an, while others emphasize the inherent mystery and awe associated with the Divine name. The chapter itself follows with a detailed discourse on divine power, the Prophets' stories, and warnings against disbelief.  Ultimately, the purpose is to strengthen faith and encourage belief through the recital and reflection on the revelations.
orig: يس

translation: And the wise Qur'an
interpretation: This verse, a single phrase, is a common introductory or concluding phrase in many discussions about the Quran. It highlights the Quran's characteristic of wisdom.  The word 'Hakeem' (حكيم)  in Arabic means wise, judicious, insightful, and possessing sound judgment.  The phrase emphasizes that the Quran is not just a book of revelations but a meticulously structured guide to life, replete with profound wisdom and guidance for humanity. It suggests a divine source and flawless logical coherence. It points to the Quran's ability to address complex human issues with clarity, prudence, and foresight, and implies a source of practical wisdom for all aspects of life.  It is the wisdom behind the verses that is being emphasized, not just the mere words themselves.  This characteristic of wisdom is a critical element in understanding and applying the Quran's teachings.
orig: والقرآن الحكيم

translation: Indeed, you are among the messengers.
interpretation: This verse, a direct address to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), affirms his prophethood and places him within the lineage of prophets sent by God throughout history.  It acknowledges his unique role and the weight of his mission.  The phrase "among the messengers" (min al-mursaleen) emphasizes that he is not an isolated or singular figure, but part of a chain of divine communication.  It underscores the continuity and consistency of God's message, delivered through various prophets throughout the ages.  Importantly, the term 'messenger' (rasul) signifies a prophet with a specific, divine revelation to convey to humanity. This verse is therefore a foundational declaration of the Prophet's role as a messenger of God, highlighting his importance within the larger prophetic narrative.
orig: إنك لمن المرسلين

translation: On a straight path.
interpretation: This verse, "على صراط مستقيم" (ʿalā ṣirāṭ mustaqīm), is a fundamental phrase in the Quran.  It literally translates to "on a straight path."  However, its meaning transcends a simple geographical description of a route.  It signifies a path of righteousness, guidance, and the correct way of life as prescribed by God.  It refers to the straight path of Islam, the way of submission to God's will, and the path leading to His pleasure and ultimate success in the Hereafter.  It encourages Muslims to strive for moral excellence, adhere to Islamic teachings, and avoid deviation from God's guidance.  The phrase is a recurring theme in the Quran, reminding believers of their purpose and the importance of seeking divine guidance in their daily lives.
orig: على صراط مستقيم

translation: A revelation from the Exalted, the Merciful.
interpretation: This verse, a common opening phrase in many Quranic verses, emphasizes the source and nature of the revelation.  "تنزيل" (tanzil) signifies a sending down, a revelation, or a bestowal.  "العزيز" (al-`Aziz) refers to God's power, strength, and majesty. "الرحيم" (ar-Rahman) denotes God's compassion, mercy, and benevolence.  The verse thus establishes that the Quran is a divine revelation originating from a powerful and merciful God. It's a statement of divine authority and the inherent goodness that permeates the message.  In essence, it signifies that the Quran is not just a human work, but a divine gift meant to guide and benefit humankind.
orig: تنزيل العزيز الرحيم

translation: That you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned, so they are heedless.
interpretation: This verse highlights the crucial role of the Prophet in conveying the message of Islam to a community that has forgotten or neglected the warnings of previous prophets.  It emphasizes the fact that the recipients of the message are in a state of negligence and obliviousness regarding the divine guidance.  The phrase 'whose fathers were not warned' suggests a generational disconnect, a failure to transmit the message of God from one generation to the next, leading to a present-day situation of spiritual apathy and ignorance.  The Prophet is therefore tasked with delivering a fresh warning, a new call to remember the consequences of disobedience and the rewards of submission to God.  The overall message underscores the enduring importance of reminding people of the divine message and the consequences of ignoring it, across generations.
orig: لتنذر قوما ما أنذر آباؤهم فهم غافلون

translation: The word has certainly become due against most of them; therefore, they do not believe.
interpretation: This verse expresses the inevitability of divine judgment and the consequences of disbelief for a significant portion of humanity.  It highlights a profound truth about the human condition—that many people, despite the clear evidence and messages presented to them, choose not to believe.  The "word" (al-qawl) here likely refers to the message of Islam, the divine decree, or the promised consequences of actions.  The fact that the word 'has become due' (laqad haqq al-qawl) emphasizes the imminent and just nature of God's judgment. The phrase "most of them" (aktharuhum) signals that this judgment extends to a large segment of society, not just a select few. The verse doesn't specifically detail the nature of the disbelief, but it underscores the significant spiritual failure that precedes divine reckoning.
orig: لقد حق القول على أكثرهم فهم لا يؤمنون

translation: Indeed, We have placed collars on their necks, so they reach to their chins. They are distressed.
interpretation: This verse describes a punishment, likely metaphorical, imposed on those who have disobeyed God. The "collars" symbolize a heavy burden, a constraint, and a sense of oppression. The phrase "so they reach to their chins" emphasizes the severity and tightness of this constraint.  It visually represents the complete restriction and frustration that this punishment brings.  'They are distressed' further emphasizes the psychological and physical suffering experienced by those subjected to this divine judgment.  The exact nature of the disobedient group and the specific form of the collars are left open to interpretation. The context of the surrounding verses would be crucial to fully understand the intended meaning and scope of this punishment. This could refer to a spiritual constriction or a physical oppression imposed in the afterlife, depending on the broader context of the Surah (chapter) it appears in. The image evokes a feeling of hopelessness and the weight of their actions.
orig: إنا جعلنا في أعناقهم أغلالا فهي إلى الأذقان فهم مقمحون

translation: And We placed a barrier in front of them and a barrier behind them, and We covered them over, so they do not see.
interpretation: This verse describes a state of blindness or ignorance imposed upon a group of people.  The "barriers" symbolize obstacles preventing them from understanding or recognizing the truth, either by blocking access to knowledge or by obscuring their minds to it.  The phrase "We covered them over" emphasizes the complete nature of this ignorance.  It's not just a temporary limitation, but a state of being effectively shielded from the light of truth.  The context is crucial for determining *who* these people are.  The verse could refer to individuals, a community, or even a historical event in which God, according to the Qur'an, put certain obstacles in the way of understanding truth.  The important point is that this ignorance is not simply a natural lack of comprehension, but something actively imposed, potentially as a consequence of their actions or choices, or perhaps as a divine judgment.
orig: وجعلنا من بين أيديهم سدا ومن خلفهم سدا فأغشيناهم فهم لا يبصرون

translation: It is the same for them whether you warn them or not; they will not believe.
interpretation: This verse expresses the unwavering nature of disbelief.  It highlights a fundamental aspect of faith and human agency.  Essentially, it states that the effectiveness of a call to faith, or the lack thereof, doesn't change the outcome for those who are determined not to believe.  Those who are destined for disbelief will remain so, regardless of any effort to guide or warn them.  The verse emphasizes that true faith is not contingent on external factors, but originates from a personal conviction and willingness to accept God's message.  It is a matter of the heart.  It doesn't diminish the importance of conveying the message, but rather acknowledges the limits of human influence on those who are hardened against it. The focus is on the inherent will and determination of individuals, and their personal choice regarding acceptance or rejection of the message.
orig: وسواء عليهم أأنذرتهم أم لم تنذرهم لا يؤمنون

translation: You are only a warner to those who follow the Reminder and fear the Most Compassionate in the unseen. So give him good tidings of forgiveness and a generous reward.
interpretation:
This verse emphasizes the role of the Prophet (peace be upon him) as a warner.  It's not about forcing belief, but rather guiding those who are receptive.  The key aspects are: 

1. **Following the Reminder (ذكر):**  This refers to the message of Islam, the Qur'an, and the teachings of the Prophet. It implies active engagement and internalization of the message, not just passive hearing.  Those who follow this reminder show a willingness to change their lives in accordance with its principles.

2. **Fearing the Most Compassionate (الرحمن) in the unseen (بالغيب):** This highlights the importance of piety, not just in visible actions, but also in inner intentions.  Fear of the unseen, in this context, signifies a deep respect for God's judgment and a realization that God is aware of all actions, even the hidden ones.  It implies a genuine understanding of God's attributes of mercy and justice.  This internalization leads to a conscious effort to live a righteous life.

3. **Good tidings of forgiveness and a generous reward:**  The verse promises a positive outcome for those who meet these criteria. This is a powerful incentive for seeking guidance and a reminder that God is merciful and generous to those who strive to please Him. The promise of forgiveness is crucial, acknowledging that everyone makes mistakes.  The 'generous reward' signifies both worldly and spiritual benefits, highlighting the enduring value of a life lived in accordance with God's guidance.
orig: إنما تنذر من اتبع الذكر وخشي الرحمن بالغيب فبشره بمغفرة وأجر كريم

translation: Indeed, it is We who give life to the dead and record what they have sent before and their traces. And every thing have We enumerated in a clear Book.
interpretation: This verse highlights the absolute power and knowledge of God. It asserts that God alone brings the dead back to life, demonstrating His complete dominion over life and death.  Crucially, it also emphasizes God's meticulous record-keeping. He meticulously records every deed, action, and trace of the past, encompassing everything from the smallest to the grandest of human endeavors.  The phrase "in a clear Book" (Imam Mubin) refers to the divine record, the Book of Deeds, which is a testament to God's justice and the accountability of humanity.  This encompasses not only actions but also the intentions, consequences, and overall impact of each person's life.  The implication is that nothing is hidden from God and all will be judged and accounted for.  This verse carries a message of profound reassurance for the believer – God's knowledge is perfect and His judgment is just. This is a powerful message of God's absolute power over the universe, His detailed record of human actions, and the ultimate accountability that awaits everyone.
orig: إنا نحن نحيي الموتى ونكتب ما قدموا وآثارهم وكل شيء أحصيناه في إمام مبين

translation: And set forth for them an example [of the people] of the town when the messengers came to it.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-A'raf, is a general framework for narrating stories of previous communities.  It introduces the concept of a specific town, visited by messengers.  The core implication is that the messengers were sent with divine messages, likely warnings about impending judgment or punishment. The use of the word "misal" (example) indicates that the story is not merely historical, but a paradigm for the current community the Quran is addressing. It's a call to learn from the mistakes and failures of those before them.  The verse sets the stage for a narrative of defiance, disbelief, and eventual retribution. The reader is prompted to consider the consequences of rejecting the messengers' guidance.  Ultimately, it serves as a warning about the potential fate of a community that ignores divine revelation.
orig: واضرب لهم مثلا أصحاب القرية إذ جاءها المرسلون

translation: When We sent to them two, they denied them, so We reinforced them with a third. They said, "Indeed, we are messengers sent to you."
interpretation: This verse describes a pattern of divine communication and response to denial.  It portrays a scenario where two messengers were sent to a people.  Their message was rejected.  In response to this rejection, Allah reinforced their message by sending a third messenger.  This act of reinforcement emphasizes the consistency and strength of the divine message.  The ultimate message conveyed by the third messenger is their declared status as messengers of Allah. This pattern illustrates that Allah’s message is persistent and will be presented in various ways, despite resistance, until it is accepted or the people are held accountable for rejecting it.  It also highlights the importance of multiple lines of evidence in conveying truth.
orig: إذ أرسلنا إليهم اثنين فكذبوهما فعززنا بثالث فقالوا إنا إليكم مرسلون

translation: They said, "You are only human beings like us, and the Most Gracious One has not sent down anything. You are only liars."
interpretation: This verse reflects a common response from those who disbelieved in the prophethood of Muhammad (peace be upon him).  They challenged the Prophet and his companions, arguing that they were ordinary people, no different from themselves.  They rejected the idea that the Quran was a divine revelation, claiming it was a fabrication.  The verse highlights the fundamental disbelief of the opponents in the divine message and their perceived superiority over the Prophet and his community, considering them to be merely human and not divinely inspired figures.  Their denial of the revelation is emphasized by the statement "You are only liars.", asserting the Quran's truthfulness in opposition to their claims.
orig: قالوا ما أنتم إلا بشر مثلنا وما أنزل الرحمن من شيء إن أنتم إلا تكذبون

translation: They said, "Our Lord, we know that we are sent to you,"
interpretation: This verse reflects the declaration of the messengers (prophets) of God.  They, recognizing their divinely appointed mission, acknowledge to God their role as messengers.  The phrase "Our Lord" (Rabbana) emphasizes their deep submission and reliance on God.  The acknowledgment "We know that we are sent to you" signifies their understanding of their duty and their acceptance of God's command.  It implies a complete awareness of the responsibility they carry in conveying God's message to humanity.  The context is crucial.  This passage likely appears in a situation where the messengers are presenting their credentials or facing opposition, affirming their divine authority to those to whom they are sent.
orig: قالوا ربنا يعلم إنا إليكم لمرسلون

translation: Upon us is only the clear exposition.
interpretation: This verse, a common theme in the Quran, emphasizes the role of the Prophet Muhammad and the revelation of the Quran as messengers of God.  It affirms that the responsibility of conveying the message rests solely with God's messengers.  They are not responsible for the recipients' faith or understanding of the message.  The role is to deliver the clear, unambiguous message (al-balagh al-mubin).  The 'clear exposition' (al-balagh al-mubin) signifies the Quran's clarity and comprehensiveness.  It is God who ultimately judges the hearts and actions of those who hear the message, not the messengers themselves. The verse underscores the divine origin and authority of the Quran, while acknowledging the human role in conveying it.
orig: وما علينا إلا البلاغ المبين

translation: They said, 'We are struck with bad omens by you. If you do not desist, we will stone you and a painful punishment will befall you from us.'
interpretation: This verse describes a situation where a group of people are rejecting and threatening a prophet or a group of people they believe to be bringing harm or misfortune.  The phrase "we are struck with bad omens by you" (قالوا إنا تطيرنا بكم) highlights the superstitious or fearful reaction of the group.  They see the prophet or group as a source of bad luck, a harbinger of misfortune, rather than looking at the message or the person themselves objectively.  The threat of stoning (لنرجمنكم) and "a painful punishment" (ليمسنكم منا عذاب أليم) is a strong indication of their hostility and intent to suppress the message or those conveying it. The overall meaning is one of rejection, fear, and the use of threats as a method of silencing a message or person they deem undesirable.
orig: قالوا إنا تطيرنا بكم لئن لم تنتهوا لنرجمنكم وليمسنكم منا عذاب أليم

translation: They said, 'Your bird is with you. If you remember (it), will you be reminded? But you are indeed a people who commit excess.'
interpretation: This verse, found in the Quran, likely refers to a specific event where a community or group was challenged regarding their actions. The phrase "Your bird is with you" likely alludes to a miraculous or symbolic bird associated with their prophet or leader, and/or perhaps an extraordinary ability that was bestowed upon them. The response of the community, "if you remember (it), will you be reminded?", implies that despite the undeniable presence of the miraculous event or capacity, they were either ungrateful, dismissive, or excessively focused on worldly pursuits, failing to recognize the deeper lessons and guidance it offered.  The concluding part, "But you are indeed a people who commit excess," serves as a strong rebuke. It highlights their detrimental lack of gratitude, their transgression against the divine will and their reckless indulgence in worldly affairs, potentially indicating a severe lack of faith or understanding. The overall implication is that the presence of divine intervention or a miraculous event does not guarantee adherence to the right path and that despite signs, some communities can remain steadfast in their excessive behaviors and neglect of spiritual guidance.
orig: قالوا طائركم معكم أئن ذكرتم بل أنتم قوم مسرفون

translation: And a man came running from the farthest part of the city, saying, "O my people, follow the messengers!"
interpretation: This verse describes a crucial moment in a community facing a critical juncture. A messenger, or prophet, has arrived to deliver a divine message.  This individual, running from a distance, highlights the urgency and importance of the message. The phrase "from the farthest part of the city" emphasizes the messenger's dedication and the significant effort he took to spread the message. It emphasizes that he traveled extensively or perhaps risked his safety and well-being, even coming from a place where the call of faith might have been the most unwelcome. His words, "O my people, follow the messengers," are a call to action, a plea to heed the divine guidance that is being offered. The verse suggests that the community has a choice: to follow the path of guidance or to reject it.  It could also be a statement about the persistence of the messenger, who continues his mission despite adversity. The verse implies a community that is aware of the messengers and their mission, but is perhaps hesitant or resistant, requiring the messenger to make a strong and persuasive plea.  The overall message conveys the divine imperative to follow those who have been sent with the truth.
orig: وجاء من أقصى المدينة رجل يسعى قال يا قوم اتبعوا المرسلين

translation: Follow those who ask you for no reward, while they are rightly guided.
interpretation: This verse encourages seeking guidance from those who are genuinely motivated by the pursuit of truth and righteousness, rather than those who seek personal gain or material rewards.  It implies that genuine guidance comes from those who are selfless and sincere in their intentions.  The verse highlights the importance of distinguishing between those who offer guidance out of selflessness and those who seek personal profit from it.  It suggests a higher standard for those who claim to guide others; they should be driven by a desire to lead others to the truth, not by a desire for material or social gain. The 'rightly guided' (مهتدون) part implies that the people being referred to are walking a righteous path and therefore are suitable examples for following. This verse is a reminder to evaluate the motives behind those who offer guidance and to prioritize those who act out of sincere intentions for the betterment of others.
orig: اتبعوا من لا يسألكم أجرا وهم مهتدون

translation: And what is to prevent me from worshipping the One who created me, and to Him you will all return?
interpretation: This verse, a powerful assertion of faith, is a rhetorical question.  It directly addresses the inherent necessity of worshipping God, the Creator. The speaker, likely a believer grappling with doubt or temptation, asks 'what could possibly hold me back?' from worshipping the very Being who brought them into existence.  The added phrase, 'and to Him you will all return,' reinforces the concept of ultimate accountability.  It highlights the inevitable return to God for judgment and emphasizes the futility of denying or neglecting this fundamental truth.  The verse isn't merely a statement of belief but also a powerful reflection on the fundamental relationship between creator and creation.  It urges the acceptance of God's authority and the reality of the hereafter as the ultimate destination.
orig: وما لي لا أعبد الذي فطرني وإليه ترجعون

translation: Shall I take besides Him (God) other deities? If the Most Gracious intends harm for me, their intercession will not avail me at all, nor will they rescue me.
interpretation: This verse powerfully emphasizes the absolute and exclusive oneness of God (Allah).  It rejects the idea of associating partners with God or relying on intermediaries to seek His favor or protection.  The speaker, likely a prophet or believer, asserts that even if other deities were present, they would be powerless to influence God's decree, especially concerning harm.  The verse highlights the futility of seeking help from anyone besides God, as only He has the power to bestow or withhold mercy, protection, and even the absence of harm.  The emphasis is on the ultimate sovereignty and absolute control that God has over all aspects of existence.
orig: أأتخذ من دونه آلهة إن يردن الرحمن بضر لا تغن عني شفاعتهم شيئا ولا ينقذون

translation: Indeed, I am then in manifest error.
interpretation: This verse, found in the Quran, expresses a profound state of spiritual turmoil and a recognition of error.  The speaker, likely a prophet or messenger of God, acknowledges a period of profound doubt or deviation from the correct path.  'In manifest error' (في ضلال مبين) signifies that the error is not subtle or hidden, but clear and evident to the speaker.  This confession isn't a sign of weakness but rather an honest admission of the human struggle with doubt and temptation.  It highlights the importance of seeking guidance and reaffirmation from God, as well as the prophet's own vulnerability and dependence on divine intervention.  It's a testament to the concept that even those chosen by God are not immune to the trials of faith. The specific context of this verse is vital for a complete understanding. Without additional information, this is a general interpretation.
orig: إني إذا لفي ضلال مبين

translation: Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen.
interpretation: This verse, often cited in the context of prophethood, expresses a declaration of faith and a call to listen. The speaker, likely a prophet or someone acting in his or her capacity, declares their complete faith in God (your Lord).  The "listen" part isn't just an instruction to hear words, but rather to heed and understand the message being conveyed. It signifies a commitment to the revealed truth and a request for the audience to do the same.  The message, as conveyed by the speaker, is presented as crucial and worthy of complete attention and acceptance, as faith (imaan) is the necessary first step in a faithful relationship with God. In the context of the Qur'an, it encourages obedience to God's commandments and submission to His will, as communicated through the prophet.
orig: إني آمنت بربكم فاسمعون

translation: It was said, "Enter Paradise." He said, "Oh, if only my people knew!"
interpretation: This verse, found in several chapters of the Quran, likely refers to a prophet or righteous individual who has been granted Paradise.  The statement of "Enter Paradise" signifies the ultimate reward for piety and obedience to God.  The exclamation, "Oh, if only my people knew!" expresses a profound longing, a deep sorrow, and a sense of profound responsibility.  The individual likely yearns for his or her community to understand and embrace the truth and teachings that led to their own salvation. The verse highlights the importance of conveying the message of God's guidance and the potential consequences of rejecting it, thereby emphasizing the prophet's sincere desire to help his community and the heavy responsibility of prophethood. It suggests a profound loss and a fervent plea for the people to understand the blessings that await those who follow God's path.
orig: قيل ادخل الجنة قال يا ليت قومي يعلمون

translation: Because my Lord has forgiven me and made me one of the honored ones.
interpretation: This verse expresses gratitude and humility. The speaker, likely the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), acknowledges the profound grace of God in forgiving their sins.  The phrase "and made me one of the honored ones" signifies not just a social or material elevation, but a spiritual distinction and a privilege granted by God.  It highlights the concept of God's favor and mercy, extending beyond mere forgiveness to bestowing honor and esteem.  The speaker recognizes their elevated position as a consequence of divine grace and not due to their own merit.  It's a testament to the power of God's forgiveness and a declaration of complete reliance on His mercy.
orig: بما غفر لي ربي وجعلني من المكرمين

translation: And We sent no army down upon his people after him from the sky, and We were not sending any.
interpretation: This verse, found in the Quran, asserts that God did not send an army from the sky to punish the people mentioned in the preceding verses.  It emphasizes God's justice and the fact that the punishment was meted out through natural or human means.  It serves as a statement of God's power, demonstrating that the punishment was not dependent on celestial intervention, but was a consequence of the people's actions.  It also signifies that Divine punishment is often gradual and not necessarily swift, and delivered via events, not divine armies.
orig: وما أنزلنا على قومه من بعده من جند من السماء وما كنا منزلين

translation: It was only a single cry, and then they were extinguished.
interpretation: This verse describes a sudden, devastating event that results in the complete annihilation of a group of people. The single cry likely symbolizes a powerful, decisive judgment or a catastrophic event that swiftly overwhelms them.  The phrase "extinguished" (khamidun) implies a complete and final cessation of existence, highlighting the swift and absolute nature of the event.  The context in which this verse appears is crucial to understanding its specific application, but it generally portrays a swift, final judgment that leaves no survivors.  Different interpretations exist based on the specific historical or metaphorical context the verse relates to within the Qur'an. It could refer to a defeat in battle, the destruction of a community, or a symbolic representation of the ultimate reckoning on the Day of Judgment.
orig: إن كانت إلا صيحة واحدة فإذا هم خامدون

translation: Woe to the servants (of Allah)! No Messenger comes to them but they ridicule him.
interpretation: This verse expresses profound sadness and disappointment regarding the human response to divine messengers.  It highlights the persistent tendency of humanity to scoff and mock those who bring guidance and warnings from God. The phrase "Woe to the servants" signifies the severe consequence of this rejection, implying a loss, a regret, and a waste of opportunity.  The verse isn't necessarily about a specific group or time period, but is a timeless lament for the general human inclination to resist truth when it is presented, regardless of the messenger.  It underscores the profound importance of listening to and accepting divine revelation, and the potential for spiritual and temporal loss that arises from rejecting it.  The mockery of messengers, the verse suggests, is a characteristic of humanity that continues throughout history and that inevitably leads to suffering and remorse.
orig: يا حسرة على العباد ما يأتيهم من رسول إلا كانوا به يستهزئون

translation: Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them? They will not return to them.
interpretation: This verse serves as a powerful reminder of the cyclical nature of history and the ephemeral nature of worldly power.  It emphasizes that past civilizations, despite their achievements and apparent permanence, eventually met their demise.  The 'destruction' referred to here is not merely physical annihilation but also the loss of their societal structures, values, and accomplishments.  The phrase "they will not return to them" highlights the irreversible nature of this process.  It is a warning to those living in the present, urging them to reflect on the fate of those who came before and to strive for righteousness and piety, lest they also meet a similar fate.  The verse underscores the importance of learning from the past and taking heed of the lessons of history.  It reinforces the idea that Allah's judgment is absolute and that all things are ephemeral in this world compared to the eternal life promised in the hereafter.
orig: ألم يروا كم أهلكنا قبلهم من القرون أنهم إليهم لا يرجعون

translation: And indeed, all of them will be present before Us.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the divine knowledge and control over all things.  It asserts that every single creature, every action, every moment, is meticulously recorded and present before God.  It's not just a statement of knowledge, but also implies accountability.  Everything that has happened, is happening, and will happen is accounted for and known to God.  This understanding is central to Islamic theology, underpinning concepts of divine judgment and the Day of Resurrection.  The verse speaks to the omnipresence and omniscience of God, highlighting His absolute control over the universe and all its inhabitants.  It is a powerful reminder that nothing escapes His notice.
orig: وإن كل لما جميع لدينا محضرون

translation: And a sign for them is the dead earth; We give it life and bring forth from it grain, from which they eat.
interpretation: This verse highlights a powerful example of God's power and provision.  It speaks to the seemingly lifeless nature of barren land, contrasting it with the abundance of life that emerges from it.  The phrase "dead earth" isn't meant literally, but rather refers to land that appears lifeless and unproductive.  The subsequent actions, "We give it life... and bring forth grain," demonstrate God's ability to create life and produce sustenance from seemingly nothing.  The verse serves as a reminder of divine providence and the continuous cycle of creation and provision. It emphasizes the connection between God's actions and the sustenance of humanity.  The grain, a basic source of food, is specifically mentioned to underscore its importance for human survival.  The overall message is one of gratitude and recognition of God's sustaining power, showcasing the beauty and wonder of God's creation. It also potentially hints at the wider cycle of death and rebirth, a recurring theme in Islamic thought, underscoring God's control over the natural world.
orig: وآية لهم الأرض الميتة أحييناها وأخرجنا منها حبا فمنه يأكلون

translation: And We placed therein gardens of palm trees and grapes, and caused springs to gush forth therein.
interpretation: This verse describes a characteristic of the blessed land, likely Paradise, or a place comparable to it.  The imagery of 'gardens of palm trees and grapes' signifies abundance, richness, and exquisite beauty. The mention of 'springs gushing forth' emphasizes the continuous and abundant source of fresh water, highlighting the prosperity and life-sustaining nature of this place. It suggests a landscape teeming with natural resources and fulfilling all the needs of its inhabitants. The verse paints a vivid picture of a place of tranquility, plentiful provision, and divine grace.
orig: وجعلنا فيها جنات من نخيل وأعناب وفجرنا فيها من العيون

translation: So that they may eat from its fruit and what their hands have worked.  Will they not give thanks?
interpretation: This verse highlights the blessings and provision of Allah (God).  It speaks to the abundance of sustenance provided in the fruits of the earth and the rewards of one's labor.  The implicit question, "Will they not give thanks?", serves as a reminder of the crucial importance of gratitude.  This principle underscores the Islamic concept of appreciating Allah's bounty in every aspect of life, encompassing both the natural world and the fruits of human effort.  The verse encourages reflection on the blessings received and the need to acknowledge Allah's role in providing them. It is a fundamental aspect of Islamic faith to recognize and express gratitude for the blessings of sustenance, recognizing that these are gifts from Allah and not simply a product of human effort alone.
orig: ليأكلوا من ثمره وما عملته أيديهم أفلا يشكرون

translation: Glory be to the One who created all pairs, from what the earth produces and from themselves and from what they do not know.
interpretation: This verse, a common theme in the Quran, highlights the vastness and complexity of God's creation.  It emphasizes the omnipotence of God in crafting pairs – not just among visible creatures (plants, animals), but also in ways humans cannot fully comprehend.  The phrase "from what the earth produces" refers to the natural world, the visible biological diversity.  The phrase "from themselves" likely alludes to the unseen processes of procreation and the intricacy of genetics. Finally, the phrase "from what they do not know" hints at the profound aspects of creation that are beyond human comprehension—subtleties of biological mechanisms, microscopic life, cosmic phenomena, and the intricate interplay of causes and effects. The verse serves as a powerful reminder of God's artistry, encompassing the visible and the invisible, the known and the unknown, all under His masterful design and control. It evokes awe and wonder at the scale and complexity of God's creation, and encourages contemplation and humility in the face of the divine artistry.
orig: سبحان الذي خلق الأزواج كلها مما تنبت الأرض ومن أنفسهم ومما لا يعلمون

translation: And a sign for them is the night, from which We strip the day, and then they are plunged into darkness.
interpretation: This verse highlights the cyclical nature of day and night as a divine sign.  The phrase "strip the day" emphasizes the transition from light to darkness, a gradual process symbolized by the sunset and the encroaching night.  It also speaks to the way darkness, with its potential for introspection and reflection, is integral to the divine order.  The verse implies a profound interconnectedness between these contrasting states – light and darkness, day and night, representing  elements of life and the divine's orchestration of the cosmos.  The phrase "and then they are plunged into darkness"  doesn't necessarily imply a state of despair or negativity. Instead, it suggests the natural, cyclical, and recurring transition into darkness, highlighting the temporary and predictable nature of this state. This darkness, preceding the dawn of a new day, is part of a greater pattern, and thus, a reminder of the divine power behind creation and its regularity.
orig: وآية لهم الليل نسلخ منه النهار فإذا هم مظلمون

translation: And the sun runs to a [predetermined] resting place. That is the decree of the Exalted in Might, the Knowing.
interpretation: This verse highlights the precision and order inherent in the universe.  It describes the sun's consistent journey across the sky, not as a random movement, but as a calculated and predetermined path.  This suggests a divine design and the power of a Supreme Being who establishes and maintains the cosmos's intricate workings.  The phrase "Exalted in Might, the Knowing" attributes these qualities to God, emphasizing His absolute control and comprehensive knowledge of all things, encompassing even the seemingly simple mechanics of celestial bodies.  The verse speaks to the concept of divine order and precision in creation, demonstrating God's meticulous care in the functioning of the universe.
orig: والشمس تجري لمستقر لها ذلك تقدير العزيز العليم

translation: And the moon, We have ordained stages for it until it returns like the withered old date-palm frond.
interpretation: This verse describes the cyclical nature of the moon's phases.  It highlights the meticulous precision and divine design behind the celestial movements.  The moon, like a date-palm frond, which eventually withers and dries, goes through a series of phases, gradually waxing and waning, eventually returning to a similar state in the cycle. This imagery emphasizes the cyclical, repetitive pattern of natural events and the consistent order maintained by God.  It also alludes to the inherent beauty and interconnectedness of the universe, where even celestial bodies follow a predetermined and observable trajectory.
